#728. The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have helped ants conquer the world

Around 66 million years ago, an asteroid struck Earth and brought the age of the dinosaurs to an end. The mass extinction that followed created opportunities for countless other animals to evolve and spread. Ants were among the groups that eventually became remarkably successful, and scientists have now identified a surprising genetic factor that may have helped fuel their rise.

Today, ants are the largest family of social insects, with more than 15,000 species found around the world. New research published in Science Advances suggests that their extraordinary evolutionary success was partly driven by mobile segments of DNA known as transposable elements, or "jumping genes."

The international study was led by Dr. Lukas Schrader of the Institute for Evolution and Biodiversity (IEB) at the University of Münster (Germany).

Jumping genes are pieces of DNA that can move to different locations within a genome and produce additional copies of themselves. Scientists once viewed them primarily as "genomic parasites" because, much like viruses, they can multiply without providing any clear benefit to their host. In some cases, their activity can even contribute to disease.

More recently, however, researchers have begun recognizing that these mobile genetic elements can also create opportunities for evolutionary change. The new findings suggest they played an important role in the remarkable diversification of ants.

When the scientists compared different groups of ants, they discovered that lineages containing the greatest numbers of jumping genes also tended to have the most species today.

Even more revealing was the timing of these genetic changes. The researchers found that several major ant lineages experienced separate surges in jumping gene activity during the early Paleogene (about 66 million years ago). These bursts occurred shortly before the groups began expanding into the thousands of species that exist today.

"The asteroid impact had dramatic consequences for the environment. We have now found the genomic mechanism that connects these ecological upheavals to the subsequent rapid diversification of the ants: transposable elements," explains Lukas Schrader.

Ants are not the only animals showing this evolutionary pattern. Previous studies have also identified periods of increased jumping gene activity associated with the emergence of new species in other groups, including primates and bats.

The researchers also discovered a connection between jumping genes and the expansion of gene families that allow ants to communicate through chemical signals.

Of particular importance were genes responsible for odorant receptors, which enable ants to detect and respond to smells. These receptors are essential to nearly every aspect of ant social behavior. Ants depend heavily on chemical cues to find their way through the environment, identify members of their own colonies, and coordinate activities with other ants.

The findings suggest that jumping genes may have contributed to the expansion of these sensory systems, potentially improving the ability of ants to detect and interpret the chemical messages that make their complex societies possible.

Tracing 100 Million Years of Ant Evolution

To investigate how jumping genes influenced ant evolution, the international research team examined and compared the genomes of 163 ant species. These represented twelve of the 16 ant subfamilies that survive today, providing a broad picture of the genetic diversity found across modern ants.

Using these genomic comparisons, the scientists reconstructed how transposable elements evolved and changed in activity over the past 100 million years.

Their results reveal a striking connection between ancient bursts of jumping gene activity and the later diversification of ants, suggesting that DNA sequences once dismissed as genetic parasites may have helped one of Earth's most successful insect groups flourish.

#726. Earth's ice ages may have been driven by a hidden ocean chain reaction

Scientists at the University of St Andrews have identified a previously unknown process that may help explain how Earth entered past ice ages. Their findings reveal a surprising connection between ice sheets in the Northern Hemisphere and ocean changes near Antarctica, suggesting that cooling in one part of the world could trigger a chain reaction affecting the entire planet.

The study, published in the Journal of Climate, offers a possible explanation for how growing northern ice sheets influenced ocean circulation and sea ice in the Southern Hemisphere. These southern changes are known to help reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2), an important factor in the development of ice ages. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain how processes occurring at opposite ends of the planet could be so closely connected.

One of the main forces behind Earth's past ice ages was a reduction in atmospheric CO2 as more carbon became stored in the oceans. Much of this process was controlled by changes in the Southern Ocean surrounding Antarctica. However, a major question remained unanswered: How could expanding ice sheets in the Northern Hemisphere, initially driven by natural variations in Earth's orbit, cause the distant Southern Ocean to absorb more CO2?

How Northern Ice Sheets Could Trigger Changes Near Antarctica

The researchers propose that the answer lies in the movement of ocean water between the hemispheres. As large ice sheets spread across northern regions, they cool nearby waters in the North Atlantic. Over time, these colder waters circulate southward, eventually reaching the Southern Ocean.

If the cooling is sufficiently strong, it could alter ocean circulation around Antarctica in ways that allow more CO2 to be stored beneath the ocean's surface. As atmospheric CO2 declines, the planet cools further, potentially helping intensify an ice age.

To investigate this possibility, the team used computer simulations of ocean circulation. Rather than lowering temperatures across the entire planet, they cooled only the northernmost latitudes (mimicking the effect of a large ice sheet) and examined how the Southern Ocean responded.

The results were striking. Cooling the far northern regions alone produced 74% as much CO2 drawdown as a separate simulation in which the entire planet was cooled. This suggests that temperature changes in the Northern Hemisphere could have a powerful influence on the Southern Ocean and its ability to store carbon.

A Missing Link in Earth's Ice Age Mystery

The simulations provide strong support for the proposed connection between expanding northern ice sheets and changes in the Southern Ocean. They suggest that colder water originating in the North Atlantic could eventually influence circulation around Antarctica, helping remove CO2 from the atmosphere and contributing to the global cooling associated with past ice ages.

For decades, much of the research into ice age climate changes has concentrated on the Southern Ocean because of its important role in controlling atmospheric carbon dioxide. Only more recently have scientists begun to recognize how changes in distant ocean regions might influence these processes.

Lead author Dr. Madison Shankle, from the University of St Andrews School of Earth and Environmental Science, explained the importance of the findings:

"Essentially, we've produced evidence of a plausible mechanism connecting these two far-flung puzzles pieces - Northern Hemisphere ice sheets and Southern Hemisphere ocean circulation changes leading to CO2 drawdown - which has been a tricky thing to explain in our theory of Earth's past ice ages. Our study takes the step of actually demonstrating them working in model simulations, which is a big step forward for this field."

What Ancient Ice Ages Reveal About Today's Climate

Understanding how past ice ages developed offers scientists a valuable way to study Earth's natural carbon cycle. These periods reveal how carbon dioxide moves between the atmosphere and oceans, and how changes in that balance can influence global temperatures.

By identifying another mechanism that may have helped reduce atmospheric CO2 during ancient ice ages, researchers can develop a more complete picture of how Earth's climate system operates.

That knowledge is especially important today, as scientists work to understand how the planet's oceans and other natural systems will respond to the additional carbon dioxide now entering the Earth system.

#725. ‘Ish’ Has Resonated Widely Amid “Authoritarian Turn,” Says Its BAFTA Breakthrough Writer-Director

Imran Perretta discusses his feature debut, which has traveled the festival circuit over the past year and attracted attention amid the riots in France: "It sparks a conversation."

Writer-director Imran Perretta’s debut feature film Ish has been making waves on the festival circuit and beyond for more than a year now.

And it feels like it has only become more timely. After all, it centers on racial profiling and a U.K. police stop-and-search that sets two best friends on a collision course.

Ish, which won the audience award at the 2025 Venice Critics’ Week, stars Farhan Hasnat, Yahya Kitana and Sudha Bhuchar and tells the story of Ish and Maram, two young teenagers who get confronted with police harassment and its repercussions. Its characters are often marginalized, both onscreen and off, and the film was shot in the city of Luton, near London, which often earns media coverage more for crime than other news. Related Stories News BAFTA Breakthrough U.K.: Ella Bruccoleri, Sophie Stone, Izuka Hoyle Among 21 Rising Creatives Business Canada's CBC Joins Microdrama Boom

On Wednesday, Perretta, who was previously best known as a multi-disciplinary artist, was revealed as a member of the 2026 U.K. BAFTA Breakthrough cohort, supported by Netflix.

He talked to THR about the journey of Ish, the surprises it has provided and its universal themes.

“I come from the art world, so for me, the life cycle of a film is really a new experience,” Peretta tells THR. “You really walk alongside the film for a long time. We did our festival run, and we’re still doing festivals here and there. But what I couldn’t really have imagined was what happened when the film came out [in cinemas]. I expected that to be the bookend of the whole experience, but in a weird way, it’s been a new start for the film.”The movie’s impact and performance have also blown him and others away. “It’s been so exciting because it exceeded all of our expectations in terms of the reception and what it did at the box office and all this sort of stuff,” he says. “So, I’m still pinching myself that so much can happen in a year. It’s crazy! I’m a very happy boy.”About the reactions and discussions that Ish has caused at screenings, Perretta shares: “There have been so many community screenings and activist screenings. A lot of activist-adjacent film organizations have shown the work all over the world, including in Germany, America, Russia. There are loads of places where allies have felt that there is a [chance for a] certain conversation politically and have wanted to engage with the film and show it to audiences.”For example, in Paris. “In the midst of the riots, programmers there have been desperate to show the film because I think they have this same conversation around police brutality and around the overreach of police powers in the context of community organizing,” he shares. “And it is also [timely] about the context of young people just trying to make a better reality for themselves.”

But again, the creative has been surprised. “What I didn’t expect was that it would speak to a much broader audience,” Perretta tells THR. “It has been amazing. There’s been this amazing spread of different types of audiences, from activist audiences or certainly politically engaged audiences to cinephiles, but then also ‘normal filmgoers.’ I’m super surprised in a good way and also really proud of that.”One reason may be that the themes that Ish explores feel very timely. “So many Western countries have taken this authoritarian turn where the police have been given powers that really extend beyond [traditional powers], or certainly they wield those powers in a way that feels really unjust or asymmetric, whether that’s in America, France, Italy, the U.K., wherever,” Perretta says. “And in that context the film sparks a conversation because, it’s sad to say, that is a universal experience now. And also, this idea of surveillance is a universal experience.”While the film may be set in Luton, he credits its specificity with making its themes and messages resonate around the world. Perretta would be happy to see Luton represented on screens more regularly. “That would be amazing, certainly if the stories show it fairly and truthfully,” he offers. “I would absolutely implore people to shoot in Luton because it’s just an amazing place.”What’s up next for the creative? “I’m working on some music stuff at the moment and have an [exhibition] at the Tate Britain,” namely the destructors, which “navigates the complexities of coming of age for Asian Muslim men in Britain after 9/11,” according to the Tate website.“And then I’m also back to screenwriting,” Perretta tells THR. “One that I’m writing at the moment has a lot to do with property and land and this very British idea of ownership – what it means to own something and what it means to leverage that ownership. You can chart a lot of the highs and lows – well, let’s be real, it’s lows for anyone other than the ruling class. So for me, it’s another political work about all of the friction – social, emotional, and political – that comes from this idea of ownership.”

#723. ‘Dune 3’ Production Designer Patrice Vermette Created a 55-Ton Spaceship for Sci-Fi Epic: It’s a ‘Major Spectacle’

SCAD Savannah Film Festival celebrated Variety's 10 Artisans to Watch and Creative Impact in Production Design honoree Patrice Vermette

Production designer Patrice Vermette promises the third and final instalkment in the “Dune” franchise is going to be “a major spectacle.” “You know when you go see fireworks, and they put everything in, and at the end, it’s ‘Oh, we have this one.’ It’s going to be like that,” he teases.

“Dune: Part Three” opens on Dec. 18. The film sees Timothee Chalamet return as Paul Atreides, continuing the story after his ascent to power at the end of “Part Two.” Inspired by Frank Herbert’s novel “Dune Messiah,” the action takes place 17 years after the events of the previous film and explores the consequences of Paul’s rule as emperor. Related Stories Jennifer Lopez to Release New Single ‘Proof of Love’: ‘It's a Happy Dance Song’ That Also Addresses ‘Pain and Grief When Someone’s Gone’ (EXCLUSIVE)

Vermette was this year’s recipient of Variety’s Creative Impact Award presented at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival. During a conversation with Variety’s Senior Artisans editor Jazz Tangcay, Vermette was mindful about revealing anything too specific.

The one directive he had from director Denis Villeneuve was “not to repeat sets.” And he didn’t.

Vermette shared some insight into how he pulled off the film’s opening sequence, which he says was a “crazy idea.” “The illustrations that I had made showed an expanse of black sand and ships attacking a planet.” One spaceship weighed 55 tons.

“We needed to put it underground and bury it. For the whole scene, it rains. So, we had spider rigs and touch spinners, and it’s a big battle sequence. We only built one ship that you see the interior and exterior 360 degrees. Every two days, we had a crane during the day coming in, lifting it. And obviously, we had a pump system to take all the water out.” The results, he says, are “worth it.”

Sharing their process, Vermette said, “The fun thing about working with Denis is we never want to repeat ourselves. Even though we’re in the same world.” They have a motto: “Let’s challenge each other. Let’s make it different.”

Before getting into “Dune,” Vermette talked about getting his start in the industry working on music videos. He started collaborating with a director and realized he had found his comfort zone: “I understood the vision of the director.” It also gave him an adrenaline rush.

As for working with Villeneuve, he and Vermette shared the same circle of friends and they had worked on commercials together in the early 2000s. The production designer was a huge fan, but their schedules never aligned for them to work together on a feature.

“I was supposed to do ‘Dallas Buyer’s Club,’ and Jean-Marc Vallée tells me, ‘Patrice, that movie’s going to be pushed a year.’” When Villeneuve heard that, he sent Vermette a text. Vermette recalled, “That text message changed my life.”

The two were finally able to collaborate on the 2013 film, “Enemy,” Villeneuve’s first English-language movie.

When Villeneuve proposed “Dune,” Vermette knew how much Herbert’s book meant to the filmmaker. “He started storyboarding for it when he was 15. He knew exactly where he wanted to be,” Vermette said.

After receiving the first 100 pages of the script and revisiting the book, Vermette took plenty of notes. But he also knew from their collaboration that “things need to have a reason to exist. Whether it’s ‘Sicario,’ ‘Enemy,’ ‘Dune’ or ‘Arrival,’ it needs to tell a story. If it’s an object that exists in this fantasy world, it needs to be grounded in reality.”

Discussing his process, Vermette explained it’s a collaborative process with other department heads, and together they figure their logistics out.

“Dune” required Vermette to bring the planet Giedi Prime to life. For that dark, black world of the Harkonnens, industrial septic tanks served as inspiration. He also had to build the Atreides Castle, as well as the planet of Arrakis, where he built the Imperial Nexus Laboratory.

Pulling off the lab was another challenge, but the collaborative process with cinematographer Greig Fraser and other department heads meant they could execute the scene without cheating sunlight. “Moral of the story: never give up on crazy ideas.”

If there is one takeaway from Variety’s 10 Artisans to Watch panel at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, it’s that collaboration, across all departments, is the key to strong filmmaking.

“Our favorite films and TV series are not created by soloists,” Kathleen Radomski, Chair of Production Design at SCAD, said while introducing the panel. “They take a village. Departments and sub-departments, sometimes separated by thousands of miles, are all dedicated to a singular vision. This community is the height of collaboration and the essence of the entertainment industry’s massive global footprint.”

Each year, Variety presents 10 artisans who use their varied skills to make an impact on their craft in recent movies and TV series. From big-budget blockbusters like “Project Hail Mary” to box office surprises like “Obsession,” the list celebrates talent from makeup, casting, editing, sound and music and more.

This year’s recipients included Anne Jimkes, supervising sound editor of “The Mosquito Bowl”; Aulo Licinio, animation supervisor of “Project Hail Mary”; Landon Lott, art director and concept illustrator of “Pluribus”; Blair McClendon, editor of “Clarissa”; Adam Newport-Berra, cinematographer of“The Invite” and “Club Kid”; Raül Refree, composer of “La Bola Negra”; Jessica Ronane, casting director of “Elsinore”; Allie Shehorn, make-up and hair department head/ special makeup effects department head of “Obsession”; Grace Snell, costume designer of “Sense and Sensibility”; and Danny Vermette, production designer of “Backrooms.”

The honorees joined Variety’s senior artisans editor Jazz Tangcay during the festival to break down their approaches to their respective projects and give advice to future filmmakers.

Several panelists, including Lott, echoed Radomski’s sentiment about teamwork on “Pluribus,” especially when creating and designing the ice hotel, which drew inspiration from real Norwegian ice hotels.

“There wasn’t just one person that designed this set,” Lott said. “There was a collaboration that went into it with not only the murals that were painted or carved on the wall, but with just the architecture in general.”

Jimkes collaborated closely with “The Mosquito Bowl” director Peter Berg to balance loud sound and silence to make the film “as authentic as possible of an experience for both the actors and the audience,” she said.

“It was essential that the audience was going to be in it and experiencing it along with the four main actors who portray these four real Marines or young men who back in the 1940s were all American football players,” Jimkes said.

Strong collaboration also requires frequent communication. McClendon, who was attached to “Clarissa” before filming began — a circumstance he prefers — found his early involvement and open dialogue with directors Arie and Chuko Esiri to be quintessential to his editing process.

“It was the kind of [shot] that I could only ask for because we had been talking about it for so long, and I was on it so early that I was like, “Oh, this is the exact kind of material in this thing that you’re going to want here,” McClendon said.

Refree similarly got a head start on his score for “La Bola Negra.” Directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi came to Refree requesting composition “while they were writing the script because they wanted to get inspired by the music.” He also worked closely with Penélope Cruz, who has a large performance scene in the film. “I could see her building up the character, building up how that singer would be in the film,” Refree said.

Ronane shared the same privilege of “building the world” when casting “Elsinore.” “We spend our lives interacting with actors,” she said. “I think everybody in the film I’ve seen on stage within the last two years. It’s a cast who are so well-placed to tell that story.”

For Licinio, developing and animating a celestial being from scratch for “Project Hail Mary” was a bit more challenging. “We really had to work a lot into finding this personality of Rocky, ” Licinio said. “A lot of that came on set, a lot of mannerisms, a lot of little things.” After consulting the source material from the novel of the same name by Andy Weir, they referenced old slapstick movies and silent comedy legends Charles Chaplin and Buster Keaton to “see how body language would evolve into getting into performance.”

While Rocky’s body language was a unique obstacle, one shared challenge some of these artisans faced was budgeting. “There’s this pie in the sky of what you want to do and then what you end up actually doing due to budgetary constraints,” Lott said.

Shehorn approached makeup and gory visual effects in “Obsession” with that same practicality. “We only have so much money, so how do we pull this effect off collectively as a team using each department to make it look as realistic as possible?” she said. The result was only having two takes to get it right. “They couldn’t go back to like, ‘Okay, now let’s try it again from no blood,’” she added.

For “Backrooms,” blood was not the problem, but “building the space, the sheer volume, was probably the biggest hurdle,” Vermette said. In fact, the team had to bring in a second rug that was a slightly different tone than the first because there simply wasn’t enough material. Vermette and director Kane Parsons ultimately adapted this restriction to be a symbolic transition in the film.

Snell had to adapt historical garb in “Sense and Sensibility” for a modern audience: “If you’re not familiar with how [historical garments] are worn and put together, they’re sort of on a pedestal in a way. There’s a wall up somewhat because you don’t understand these garments and what they mean. So for how I could bring everybody in was if I did contemporary styling so that you could actually see yourself in these characters. How we might wear clothing today, which might be undone or somewhat mismatched, slightly self-styled,” she said.

While they all had their unique challenges to overcome and different approaches to their individual tasks, each artisan concurred on the importance of collaboration, inviting emerging filmmakers to be kind and work together.

“Think like a filmmaker,” Jimkes said. “You need to be able to talk to a producer in their language about budgets and schedules. You need to be able to talk with a director about the story. You need to be able to talk to your coworkers, for me, sound designers, composers, in their way of speaking, in their language. Be a filmmaker, learn about all the aspects. It’ll help you navigate the politics.”

The only way to do so, Lott added, referencing Nike’s iconic slogan, is to “just do it”

“Always be making shit,” Vermette echoed. “That’s a big part of it. Just keep going. Grab your buddies, go make a film. Just never stop. You don’t get good by sitting around wishing to be good. Just go out and practice, practice, practice.”

#722. Scientists discover a hidden 100-million-year-old volcanic system

Scientists have uncovered evidence of a previously unknown volcanic system that formed roughly 100 million years ago in what is now northwestern Iran. The discovery reveals a missing chapter in the region's geological history and offers new clues about the powerful tectonic forces that shaped ancient oceans and continents.

Mountain ranges contain valuable records of Earth's distant past, preserving traces of vanished oceans, shifting continents, and the geological processes that transformed the planet over millions of years. However, these records are often difficult to interpret because later tectonic activity, erosion, and layers of buried sediment can conceal evidence of much older events.

An international team led by Istanbul Technical University (ITU) has now identified remnants of an ancient continental magmatic arc that had previously gone unrecognized. Named the Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc, the system formed during the Late Cretaceous period in a region that is now part of the Arabia-Eurasia collision zone.

The research, published in Geoscience Frontiers, indicates that the volcanic system was active approximately 101 to 97 million years ago, when the ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean was undergoing major geological changes. Over time, tectonic deformation, erosion, burial beneath sedimentary basins, and a younger episode of volcanic activity during the Eocene obscured much of the evidence of its existence.

Ancient Rocks Reveal a Lost Volcanic System

To reconstruct this overlooked chapter of Earth's history, the researchers examined volcanic and plutonic rocks collected from multiple locations across northwestern Iran. Much of their investigation focused on formations along the Siah Cheshmeh-Khoy-Misho-Tabriz Fault.

The team used several advanced techniques to determine when the rocks formed and where their original materials came from. These included zircon U-Pb geochronology to establish their ages, Hf isotope analyses to investigate their sources, and whole-rock geochemistry to examine their chemical composition.

Together, the results revealed signatures consistent with continental arc magmatism, a geological process that occurs when one tectonic plate sinks beneath another, generating magma that can rise through the overlying continental crust.

Dr. Ali Mohammadi, the study's corresponding author at Istanbul Technical University, explained: "This study shows that the magmatic history of northwestern Iran is more complex than previously recognized. By integrating geochronological, isotopic, and geochemical evidence, we identified a Late Cretaceous continental arc that was subsequently obscured by later tectonic processes."

The international research effort also involved scientists from the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research and Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences; ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Karadeniz Technical University, Türkiye; and Damghan University, Iran.

A Missing Piece of Iran's Geological History

Previous reconstructions of Iran's ancient magmatic activity have largely centered on two major geological features: the Sananda-Sirjan Magmatic Arc and the Urumieh-Dokhtar Magmatic Arc.

The newly identified Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc adds another important piece to that history. Its discovery suggests that northwestern Iran experienced a separate episode of continental arc activity during the Late Cretaceous, expanding scientists' understanding of how the region developed.

The findings also point to a potentially important role for the Siah Cheshmeh-Khoy-Misho-Tabriz Fault. Researchers suggest that this fault may mark a major tectonic boundary connected to changes in the ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean system.

Those changes may have included slab rollback, a process in which a descending tectonic plate retreats as it sinks into Earth's interior, as well as the migration of volcanic arcs to new locations. Such movements could help explain why this particular episode of magma formation lasted for a relatively short period.

New Clues About the Disappearance of an Ancient Ocean

Beyond Iran, the discovery provides a broader lesson about how Earth's geological history can become hidden over immense stretches of time.

Ancient magmatic arcs do not always survive as continuous, easily recognizable formations. Tectonic movements can break them apart, erosion can remove exposed rocks, and sedimentation can bury what remains. Later volcanic activity can further complicate the record, making older systems particularly difficult to identify.

By recognizing the surviving fragments of these ancient structures, scientists can better reconstruct how tectonic plates descended beneath one another, how volcanic arcs shifted, how continental crust grew, and how once-vast oceans eventually closed.

The Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc offers new evidence for understanding the Late Cretaceous evolution of northwestern Iran and the larger Neo-Tethyan region. It also helps researchers refine geological models of an area shaped by repeated episodes of ocean closure and continental collision.

The ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean played a major role in the geological development of the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East, and Western Asia. Its eventual disappearance helped shape the modern landscapes of these regions.

By uncovering a volcanic system that had been largely erased from the geological record, researchers have added another piece to the complex story of how Earth's continents and oceans evolved over millions of years.

#721. Are the Midterms About to Be a Blowout Ratings Night for Cable News?

Viewership took a hit in 2022, but they could bounce back to 2018 levels this year.

Whatever partisan leanings the cable news networks may or may not have, they’re likely united on one thing about Tuesday’s midterm election: They hope it’s more like 2018 than 2022.

And with Donald Trump pretend-on-the-ballot, they just might get their wish.

The 2018 midterms were dramatic, with Democrats gaining a House of Representatives majority and ending a Republican trifecta in Congress and the White House after Donald Trump’s victory in 2016 (Republicans increased their Senate majority by two seats). Democrats also flipped several governorships. News outlets offered coverage more akin to a presidential year, and it paid off in the largest collective TV audience for a midterm election night this century. Related Stories Movies Jennifer Lawrence Cites 'Hunger Games' While Encouraging Fans to Vote: "Don't Forget Who Burns With Us" Midterms 2026 The Six Wild Campaign Ads Definitely Not Destined for the Paley Center

The 2022 midterms were … not that. Republicans regained control of the House, though a pundit-forecasted “red wave” didn’t really materialize. The Senate went form a 50-50 tie to a one-seat majority for Democrats. It was a much more typical midterm outcome, with the party not in the White House making legislative gains — but not huge ones.

TV ratings reflected the differences: Across all linear networks’ coverage, the 2018 midterms averaged 36.1 million viewers, a huge increase over the 22.7 million average in 2014. The big three broadcast networks devoted all of primetime to the election, vs. just the 10 p.m. hour in 2014, contributing to the big gains.

The three biggest cable news outlets also had their best midterm night ever, both in primetime and for the full night of coverage (6 p.m.-1 a.m. ET). Fox News, CNN and MSNBC (now known as MS NOW) averaged a combined 13.94 million viewers for the full night (and more than 17 million in primetime). Fox News led the way with a seven-hour average of 6.12 million viewers, up 23 percent from 2014. CNN (3.88 million) and MSNBC (3.95 million) more than doubled their 2014 numbers.

That momentum also carried through the rest of November 2018, with total-day viewers up for all three networks compared to a year earlier. CNN and MSNBC also showed viewer gains in the first two months of 2019 as the new Congress was gaveled in, while Fox dipped some (while still maintaining a sizable overall lead). That might be a reflection of each network’s leanings: MSNBC is pretty openly liberal, and the CNN of 2018-19 was a regular target of ire for Trump and his administration.

Four years later, audiences weren’t nearly as keyed in on the midterms. The all-network average was 25.43 million viewers in primetime, down 30 percent from 2018. Fox News had the smallest ratings dip, declining by about 8 percent over the full election night block. CNN and MSNBC suffered much more, falling by 47 percent and 32 percent in total viewers.

The post-election halo was also smaller: All three had improved numbers in November 2022 vs. November 2021, and CNN and MSNBC had small-ish year-to-year gains in January 2023’s full day numbers. Those gains went by the wayside a month later, however, as all three fell vs. February 2022 — when news viewing surged with the start of the Russia-Ukraine war.

The pre-election narrative this year seems to be leaning a little more toward the higher stakes of eight years ago than the relatively business-as-usual outcome of 2022. Ratings later this week will help tell the story — which news executives hope will be a good one.

This is part of The Hollywood Reporter’s ongoing midterm coverage. You can check out all of our pieces here.

#719. From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.

"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.

But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.

"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."

Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.

"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.

Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.

A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.

However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.

Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.

Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.

"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.

Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.

"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."

The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."

They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.

But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.

What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.

Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.

He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.

Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.

"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.

The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.

Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."

Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.

"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.

Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.

"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.

Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.

"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."

Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.

He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.

"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said. Edited by: Rosalie Delaney

#718. Scientists discover the immune system’s hidden sense of touch

Scientists at McGill University have discovered a surprising ability in immune cells that could reshape our understanding of how the body develops lasting protection against infections.

For years, researchers believed that tissue-resident memory T cells, specialized immune cells that remain in the body's tissues after an infection and respond quickly if the same threat returns, were guided mainly by chemical signals.

However, a new study published in Nature Immunology challenges that assumption. Researchers found that T cells can detect how stiff their surrounding tissues are and use this physical information to influence whether they develop into long-lasting memory cells. The findings suggest that adjusting to the stronger mechanical forces within tissues may be important for these protective cells to survive over time.

"This is an exciting fundamental finding that challenges the way we think about immune cells," said lead author Judith Mandl, a professor in McGill's Department of Physiology. "It suggests T cells can 'feel' their surroundings and adapt to them, making the physical environment an active force in shaping their behavior."

The research brought together scientists from McGill's Department of Physiology, the Alan Edwards Centre for Research on Pain, the Department of Bioengineering, and the McGill University Health Centre, along with collaborating institutions in the Netherlands and the United States.

How the Discovery Could Influence Cancer and Immune Treatments

Understanding how T cells respond to physical conditions could eventually open new possibilities for treating diseases in which the immune system mistakenly targets healthy tissue. These include autoimmune disorders, allergies, and complications involving transplant rejection.

The discovery could also have important implications for cancer research, particularly efforts to improve treatments that use the immune system to fight tumors.

"Tumors are often dense and physically difficult for immune cells to penetrate. Understanding how T cells adapt to these environments could help researchers design cancer immunotherapies that are better able to reach and attack tumors," said Mandl.

How Scientists Discovered the Immune Cells' Hidden Sense of Touch

To investigate whether physical surroundings influence T cell behavior, the researchers studied immune cells collected from humans and mice. They placed the cells inside specially designed collagen gels that mimicked tissues with different levels of stiffness.

The experiments revealed a clear pattern. As the gels became stiffer, T cells were increasingly likely to acquire characteristics associated with tissue-resident memory cells, which help provide long-term immune protection.

These results indicate that the physical properties of surrounding tissues can help shape how immune cells develop, adding an important new dimension to scientists' understanding of immune memory.

The researchers now hope to identify the specific molecular sensor that enables T cells to detect their physical environment. Determining how this sensor converts mechanical forces into changes in cell behavior could help explain how the immune system establishes lasting protection.

The study received funding from the Human Frontier Science Program, the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Canadian Foundation for Innovation, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, and the U.S. National Institutes of Health.

#717. How Jon Ossoff Won Re-Election and Became the Midterms’ Main Character in the Process

When Democrat Jon Ossoff took the stage on Tuesday night in Atlanta to declare victory in his campaign for re-election in the Senate, hours after CNN projected that he would take down his opponent, the MAGA-friendly U.S. Rep. Mike Collins, by a wide margin, he was quick to throw down the latest of his string of cutting remarks about the Trump administration.

“In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption, and incompetence of the failed, lame duck president Donald J. Trump,” he told the raucous crowd. “And if at times these last two years, amid the ceaseless onslaught of brutality and indecency, you doubted whether our republic would survive, let tonight’s results give you courage. While the more compelling Senate contests for many political observers were in the toss-up states of Maine, Michigan and Texas, Ossoff and the seemingly safe Georgia race became a fascination from inside the Beltway to the mansions of Brentwood as the midterms played out. This race had a little something for everyone.

Until recently, Ossoff was known for his 2020 runoff defeat of incumbent Republican David Perdue — a true nail-biter that grabbed global attention because his win, which was announced amid the January 6 Capitol Hill riots, meant Democrats would enter Joe Biden’s term with control of the Senate. Ossoff then laid low as a young Senate moderate who brokered some ho-hum bipartisan deals on drug prices until, in February, after an exhausting year of MAGA 2.0, the 39-year-old senator delivered a stump speech at the Georgia International Convention Center in which he characterized Trump as a “failed lame duck” who is deeply unpopular in Georgia and dubbed his administration the “Epstein class.” The speech spread widely online and brought in a wave of donations and, soon, attention from Hollywood’s elite. Now he’s one of the hottest Democrats in the country, and his declared lack of presidential ambitions hasn’t stopped chatter around a potential Ossoff 2028 bid.

How he got here is a story worth its own script treatment.

Ossoff was unopposed in the Democratic primary and spent the time sharpening his attacks on the Trump administration, hammering the president on inflation, foreign relations in the Middle East, immigration enforcement and the FBI raid that seized 2020 election documents in Fulton County. In the closing days of his reelection campaign, he questioned the objectives of the U.S. war in Iran and the administration’s official claims of military success. He cited record-high diesel prices and criticized tariffs and health care cuts. His pitch was summed up Monday at a speech in Decatur.

“We need change,” Ossoff told the crowd gathered for a final door-knocking push. “They have lied us into yet another war in the Middle East. They slashed Medicaid and doubled health insurance premiums to cut taxes for the rich. These tariffs have sent grocery prices soaring. They’re crushing Georgia’s small businesses and Georgia farms, but these next 26 hours are the time remaining for us to wield the power and the rights invested in us as citizens by our Constitution to make a difference.”

That criticism is decaf compared with what he saved for Trump himself. The first Millennial senator laid into the president in ways many would not have, alleging he preferred traveling with aide Natalie Harp and building an $800 million White House ballroom over fulfilling his presidential duties. He went on to accuse him of sleeping through meetings, golfing and trading stocks. Asked about Ossoff by the press, Trump offered a jab at his appearance, calling him a “Pee-wee Herman lookalike” and later mocking his $900 makeup session. The spat began in the context of Trump’s approval rating dipping below the 40 percent threshold and Ossoff’s polls moving up and to the right.

As the internet’s eyes turned to Ossoff over these campaign moments, Hollywood’s naturally followed, and the incumbent senator was enjoying the spoils of fundraising events held by television heavyweights Shonda Rhimes and Chuck Lorre, with maxed-out donations from Larry David, Sally Field and David Geffen, among other A-listers. The right has cried foul over these Hollywood connections in ways that seem to have fallen on deaf ears among Georgians concerned with kitchen-table issues and not whom the biz’s boomers are backing. Ossoff’s presidential ambitions are naturally questioned in this context, and as one politico reportedly told Page Six, if he bests his GOP rival today by 6 points, he’ll be all but shoved into a race against other potential 2028 Democratic favorites, California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

The polls ahead of the vote had shown Ossoff with a commanding lead well over that 6-point mark; in fact, the final average had him +10 over Collins, whose backstory is an entirely different tale that involved a split in Georgia’s GOP. It began with a last-minute endorsement from Trump ahead of the primary runoff, which Collins earned over loyalty to the MAGA movement; i.e., he echoes, to this day, Trump’s big lie about his election defeat to Joe Biden in 2020. Collins’ runoff rival, Derek Dooley, has refuted these claims, which makes sense because he’s a childhood pal of Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp; the GOP initially wanted Kemp, who is exiting the governor’s office, to run against Ossoff, despite his clashes with Trump over election fraud. Dooley stood in as a surrogate but lost the runoff to the congressman and Trump loyalist.

With Collins out of the picture, Ossoff is now firmly in main-character position. Given that magnetic stump speech and the run he’s had since February, all eyes will on the senior senator from Georgia in the coming days, and certainly not for the last time.

#715. NASA’s Artemis I mission reveals surprising radiation levels near the Moon

NASA's Artemis I mission has provided new insights into how much cosmic radiation astronauts may encounter near the Moon compared with low Earth orbit. Using experimental detectors made from lithium fluoride crystals aboard the Orion spacecraft, researchers have obtained preliminary measurements that reveal unexpected differences in radiation exposure between the two environments.

During the uncrewed Artemis I mission in late November and early December 2022, Orion traveled around the Moon carrying more than 10,000 tiny crystals embedded inside two human-shaped mannequins. These devices recorded radiation exposure throughout the journey. Among them were several dozen experimental fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors created by scientists at the Institute of Nuclear Physics of the Polish Academy of Sciences (IFJ PAN) in Cracow. The researchers have now described a new method for analyzing the information stored in these crystals, offering insights into both cosmic radiation levels and the performance of the detectors. Their findings were published in the journal Radiation Measurements.

"The fluorescent radiation dose detectors based on lithium fluoride, developed at our institute, are passive in nature. In other words, they work like photographic film: once the crystals have been exposed to radiation, the tracks left by individual particles must be analyzed optically under a microscope," explains Prof. Pawel Bilski (IFJ PAN), one of the co-authors of the paper.

How Tiny Crystals Detect Cosmic Radiation

The lithium fluoride detectors work by capturing microscopic changes caused by radiation. When electrically charged particles pass through a crystal, they disrupt its internal atomic structure, creating defects known as color centers. Scientists can later illuminate the crystal with blue light, causing these altered regions to glow red. By examining that fluorescence under a microscope, researchers can identify the paths taken by individual radiation particles.

The detectors were part of the MARE (Matroshka AstroRad Radiation Experiment) study conducted during Artemis I. Several dozen experimental lithium fluoride detectors were placed inside both mannequins, including some containing high concentrations of the lithium-7 isotope. The contribution from IFJ PAN extended beyond these experimental devices. Its scientists also supplied nearly 600 thermoluminescent crystal detectors, which use a different technique to measure radiation exposure.

One major advantage of the new lithium fluoride detectors is that they simplify the process of examining radiation tracks. Traditional passive detectors made from plastic require chemical etching before scientists can study the marks left by incoming particles. Lithium fluoride crystals eliminate that step, allowing researchers to inspect the tracks directly with a standard fluorescence microscope.

As a result, observing the radiation tracks collected near the Moon was relatively straightforward. The more difficult task was determining exactly what those tracks revealed about radiation exposure. To obtain reliable numerical measurements, the team had to develop sophisticated calibration and analysis techniques.

Why Measuring Deep Space Radiation Is So Difficult

Unlike the controlled conditions of a laboratory, cosmic radiation is highly unpredictable. In a typical physics experiment, researchers can expose a detector to a beam containing a known type of particle with a specific energy and direction. In space, radiation arrives from every direction and includes many different particles and atomic nuclei traveling across an enormous range of energies.

This complexity makes the microscopic tracks difficult to interpret. Because incoming particles strike the crystals at different angles, their tracks extend in multiple directions. A microscope captures the section of each track within its focal plane (approximately one micrometer in size), but it also records a blurry glow from portions outside that narrow region. This additional light influences the measured fluorescence intensity, which scientists use to estimate how densely a particle ionizes the material.

Different particles also produce very different track patterns. Those that cause strong ionization leave continuous, sharply defined lines, while particles that produce weaker ionization may appear as scattered, disconnected dots. These differences further complicate the task of translating fluorescence measurements into meaningful radiation data.

To overcome these challenges, the researchers introduced several corrections and developed software capable of removing unwanted background signals. The improved analysis brought their measurements into close agreement with results from established detector technologies while also revealing radiation events that older devices could not detect.

"After applying a series of corrections and developing software to appropriately remove the background interfering with the measurements, our results differed by no more than 15% from those obtained using conventional track detectors across the entire overlapping range of energy deposition values. Moreover, we also recorded numerous particle tracks corresponding to energy deposits below the detection threshold of the detectors used to date," Prof. Bilski emphasizes.

Artemis I Reveals a Surprising Difference in Moon Radiation

The Artemis I measurements also allowed researchers to compare radiation exposure near the Moon with findings from an earlier experiment aboard the International Space Station.

More than a decade before Artemis I, the MATROSHKA experiment investigated radiation exposure using human-shaped mannequins on the space station. Some of the radiation recorded during that mission came from low-energy protons trapped within Earth's Van Allen radiation belts. As these particles traveled into the mannequins, they deposited energy at different depths, producing an uneven distribution of radiation doses.

Conditions near the Moon are substantially different. The Van Allen belts do not extend into the lunar environment, so the radiation encountered there contains a greater contribution from high-energy particles originating elsewhere in the galaxy.

These galactic particles carry enough energy to travel through the entire human body, releasing only a portion of their energy as they pass. Consequently, the Artemis I detectors recorded radiation doses that were distributed almost uniformly throughout the mannequins, unlike the uneven patterns observed in the earlier space station experiment.

The researchers also identified a finding that may seem counterintuitive. Although astronauts near the Moon are exposed to more radiation than those in low Earth orbit, the difference is not necessarily as dramatic as might be assumed.

"Low-energy protons, trapped by our planet's magnetic field within the Van Allen belts, can account for the majority of the radiation dose received by astronauts in low Earth orbit. In the vicinity of the Moon, this substantial contribution disappears. Our measurements from the MARE experiment indicate that, although total radiation doses near the Moon are higher than those in Earth orbit due to the considerable levels of galactic radiation, the difference is not as large as one might intuitively expect," Prof. Bilski notes.

New Radiation Detectors Could Help Protect Future Astronauts

The fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors aboard Artemis I were manufactured using the Czochralski method, a technique for growing crystals. Scientists at IFJ PAN first developed the technology about a decade ago and have continued refining it ever since.

Their compact size is one of their most useful features. Measuring just a few millimeters rather than several centimeters (on the order of millimeters rather than centimeters), the detectors are small enough to be worn comfortably by people, making them practical for monitoring radiation exposure during space missions.

They also provide sharper images of particle tracks than conventional plastic detectors that require chemical etching. This improved resolution allows scientists to distinguish individual tracks even when radiation doses are relatively high. In addition, the crystals can register a broad variety of particle types and energies, potentially providing a more complete picture of the radiation environment.

Another advantage is their ability to detect neutrons, particularly when the crystals are enriched with the lithium-6 isotope. When neutrons interact with lithium nuclei, they can trigger nuclear reactions that generate secondary charged particles. These particles leave detectable changes in the crystal, much like other forms of ionizing radiation.

Together, these capabilities make lithium fluoride detectors a promising tool for studying the complex radiation environment beyond Earth. The measurements from Artemis I offer a clearer picture of how cosmic radiation behaves near the Moon and demonstrate how compact detectors could help scientists evaluate radiation exposure during future missions.

The research conducted as part of the MARE project was supported by a grant from the National Science Centre, Poland (NCN), under its OPUS program.

#713. Scientists discover a hidden oxygen reservoir deep inside Earth

Scientists have discovered that molten rock deep inside Earth can store far more oxygen than previously believed. The finding challenges long-standing assumptions about magma and raises an intriguing possibility: oxygen released from Earth's interior may have helped transform the planet's atmosphere billions of years ago.

Through high-pressure experiments and advanced computer simulations, researchers found that magma can absorb additional oxygen beyond the amount normally required by its chemical composition. This hidden oxygen could provide a previously unrecognized connection between Earth's deep interior, volcanic activity, and the development of an oxygen-rich atmosphere.

The research was led by Dr. Yanhao Lin and Dr. Ho-kwang Mao of the Center for High Pressure Science and Technology Advanced Research (HPSTAR), working with Prof. Haiyang Niu of Northwestern Polytechnical University and Prof. Wim van Westrenen of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Their findings were published in National Science Review.

Scientists Challenge a Long-Standing Assumption About Magma

Oxygen is one of the most abundant elements inside Earth, accounting for more than half of the atoms in the planet's silicate interior. Silicates are minerals and molten materials composed primarily of silicon and oxygen, along with other elements. They make up much of Earth's mantle and crust.

Despite oxygen's abundance, scientists have traditionally assumed that magma can contain only a specific amount of it. Under this understanding, the oxygen content is determined by the quantities and electrical charge states of other elements in the molten rock, including silicon, magnesium, and iron.

Water and carbon dioxide behave differently. Both can dissolve in magma and later escape as gases when the surrounding pressure decreases. These substances are known as volatile components, and their release plays an important role in volcanic activity.

Oxygen, however, has generally not been treated as a separate volatile substance that magma can absorb and release. Whether molten silicate rock could hold additional oxygen independently of its ordinary chemical composition remained largely unexplored.

The new research suggests that this assumption may need to change.

Extreme Pressure Reveals Hidden Oxygen in Molten Rock

To investigate, the scientists recreated conditions found deep within Earth using laboratory equipment capable of generating extraordinary pressures and temperatures.

They heated a synthetic version of mid-ocean ridge basalt, a type of volcanic rock commonly produced where tectonic plates move apart beneath the oceans. The samples were exposed to pressures ranging from normal atmospheric pressure to 7 gigapascals and temperatures between 1200 and 1800 °C.

A pressure of 7 gigapascals is approximately 69,000 times the atmospheric pressure at Earth's surface.

The team used specialized piston-cylinder and cubic presses to maintain these extreme conditions. They also added platinum oxide (PtO2) to establish an oxygen-rich environment and test how much additional oxygen the molten rock could absorb.

After the experiments, the researchers rapidly cooled the molten material, producing glass that preserved important characteristics of the melt. They then analyzed its elemental composition and measured the amounts of water and carbon dioxide present.

By calculating how much oxygen was needed to balance the other elements, along with the oxygen already contained in water and carbon dioxide, the scientists could estimate how much remained unaccounted for.

They called this additional amount "excess oxygen."

The results revealed a striking relationship between pressure and oxygen storage.

At normal atmospheric pressure, the glass contained almost no excess oxygen. At 7 gigapascals, however, excess oxygen accounted for more than 5% of the sample's weight.

For comparison, experiments conducted at similar pressures and temperatures without added platinum oxide produced excess oxygen concentrations of only 0.2% to 0.5% by weight.

The researchers also wanted to determine whether the additional oxygen was truly incorporated into the material or merely trapped as tiny gas bubbles.

Using Raman spectroscopy, a technique that identifies substances by examining how they interact with light, they found no detectable signature of oxygen gas in the glass. This indicated that the excess oxygen had become part of the glass structure rather than accumulating in bubbles.

The measured concentrations may even underestimate magma's actual oxygen-storage capacity. Some oxygen could have escaped while the molten samples were cooling, meaning the original melts may have contained still greater amounts.

Computer Simulations Reveal How Magma Stores Extra Oxygen

To better understand the discovery at the atomic level, Prof. Niu led a series of theoretical computer simulations.

The researchers used deep neural network (DNN) models to simulate interactions among atoms with accuracy approaching that of ab initio calculations, which describe atomic behavior using fundamental principles of quantum mechanics.

The simulations showed that additional oxygen could dissolve into molten material until the system reached equilibrium, a state in which oxygen entering and leaving the melt is balanced.

Although the computer models used a simplified system containing only magnesium, silicon, and oxygen, they reproduced the same overall pattern observed in the laboratory: magma's ability to hold excess oxygen increased with pressure.

The simulated oxygen concentrations were lower than the experimental measurements, which the scientists attributed to differences between the simplified model and the more complex chemical composition of actual basalt.

The calculations also revealed changes in how oxygen atoms behaved as more oxygen entered the melt. Their electrical charges became more varied, and a small proportion formed peroxide-like bonds, in which oxygen atoms bond to one another.

These changes help explain how molten rock might accommodate oxygen beyond the amount predicted by conventional chemical models.

Importantly, the pressure-dependent behavior resembles that of water and carbon dioxide, which also become more soluble in magma as pressure increases.

Based on these findings, the researchers propose that oxygen should be recognized as an independent component of silicate melts, rather than being considered only in relation to other elements.

Could Ancient Volcanoes Have Helped Oxygenate Earth's Atmosphere?

The discovery raises a much larger question about Earth's history: Could magma have transported significant amounts of oxygen from the planet's interior to its surface?

The researchers suggest a possible mechanism involving magma generated in oxidized regions of Earth's mantle.

Under the immense pressures deep underground, this magma could absorb substantial quantities of excess oxygen. As it moves upward, the surrounding pressure decreases, reducing the amount of oxygen the molten rock can retain.

Some of that oxygen could then be released, potentially contributing to chemical reactions that increase the oxidation of the upper mantle, Earth's crust, and eventually the atmosphere.

Oxidation refers to chemical processes involving the transfer of electrons. In this context, oxygen carried by magma could increase the oxidizing capacity of surrounding materials and potentially influence the balance of oxygen in the atmosphere.

This proposed mechanism may also help explain an intriguing coincidence in Earth's geological past.

Between approximately 2.5 billion and 2.0 billion years ago, atmospheric oxygen levels underwent major increases. This interval overlaps with the formation of some of Earth's largest large igneous provinces (LIPs), enormous regions of volcanic rock created by exceptionally large outpourings of magma.

The researchers suggest that oxygen released from these ancient volcanic systems could have contributed to changes in atmospheric composition.

Their preliminary calculation highlights the potentially enormous scale of the process. They estimate that if magma erupted during this period released excess oxygen equal to just 0.27% of its weight, the total amount could theoretically match all the oxygen present in Earth's atmosphere today.

This does not establish that volcanic activity actually supplied that much atmospheric oxygen. Instead, it illustrates how even a relatively small release of oxygen from immense quantities of magma could have major planetary consequences.

A New Clue to Earth's Evolution and Habitable Planets

The findings could influence several important areas of planetary science.

For one, they may change how scientists understand ancient magma oceans, vast regions of molten rock believed to have existed during the early evolution of Earth and other rocky planets.

They also introduce a possible new factor in volcanic degassing, the process through which gases and other volatile substances escape from molten rock and interact with a planet's atmosphere.

If magma can store and release oxygen independently of its other chemical components, models of Earth's atmospheric development may need to account for this previously overlooked process.

The implications could extend beyond Earth. Understanding how oxygen moves between the interiors and atmospheres of rocky planets may help researchers investigate the conditions that allow potentially habitable environments to develop and persist over billions of years.

Although further research is needed to establish how much oxygen natural magmas carry and how much reaches the atmosphere, the discovery points to a surprising possibility: some of the processes that helped shape Earth's oxygen-rich environment may have originated far beneath the planet's surface.

#712. Lucy Liu’s ‘The Pirate Queen’ Expands With Graphic Novel, New Game and International Tour as Creator Eloise Singer Joins BAFTA Breakthrough Cohort (EXCLUSIVE)

Lucy Liu and Eloise Singer are preparing to take “The Pirate Queen: No Safe Waters,” their immersive experience about Chinese pirate leader Cheng Shih, on an international tour next year, Singer tells Variety. The pair have also co-written a graphic novel and are developing a new game.

The news comes as Singer, the project’s writer and director, joins the 2026 BAFTA Breakthrough U.K. cohort. Related Stories James Wan and Jason Blum Unveil New Company Name: Blumhouse Atomic Keanu Reeves in Talks to Star in James Wan's ‘The Gangster, The Cop, The Devil’ at Paramount

The franchise is built around a retelling of the stories about real life character Cheng Shih, who was a powerful female pirate in the South China Sea at the beginning of the 18th century.

“No Safe Waters” played in the Cannes Film Festival’s Immersive Competition this year, with Liu narrating and producing alongside Singer. It follows the original 2024 VR version of “The Pirate Queen,” which earned an Emmy nomination.

Liu says Cheng Shih was intelligent and strategically brilliant, and won respect through negotiation and leadership “in a world designed to exclude women entirely.” In Liu’s view, the pirate leader defies nearly every stereotype historically placed on Asian women in storytelling. “She was politically astute, ruthless when necessary, deeply strategic, and completely self-determined. Stories like hers remind us that history has always contained powerful, complex women – they were never centered in mainstream narratives,” Liu tells Variety. “That’s beginning to change, and I think audiences are hungry for stories that feel more expansive.”

Where the first outing was built for a headset, the new piece fills a shared room with projection, sound and movement. Audiences stand among storms and fleets as dragons move beneath their feet.

Liu does not appear on screen. She says voice carries a different kind of responsibility in immersive work, guiding atmosphere and movement at the same time. “In film, the camera captures a glance or physical gesture to communicate subtext, but here the voice can help create emotional architecture,” she says.

Singer has spent a decade on “The Pirate Queen,” the last three years of it with Liu, and says the pair have co-written a graphic novel, are preparing the international tour and are developing a new game. “I feel really lucky to be making it with Lucy. She’s thrown her heart and soul into this alongside me, and getting to build this world together has been one of the most special parts of the journey,” she says. “I love seeing how one story can take on a whole new life across different formats, each offering audiences a completely different way to experience it.”

Liu says the project’s ambition, and the importance of telling Cheng Shih’s story with nuance and scale, is something she and Singer both care about deeply. “We’re building ‘The Pirate Queen’ as a larger storyworld together, so it was never just about lending my voice to one experience,” she says. “As a producer, I wanted to help support the integrity of the story and the larger creative vision. I’m always drawn to work that challenges convention and creates space for voices and histories that haven’t been fully explored, and Cheng Shih’s story deserves that kind of scale.”

BAFTA named Singer to this year’s Breakthrough program, its Netflix-supported initiative for emerging screen talent, on Nov. 4. She was selected in the games category for “No Safe Waters.”

“It’s still a bit of a pinch-me moment. It’s something I’ve aspired to for such a long time, so to be selected is a little surreal, and to have BAFTA and Netflix recognize what we’ve created with ‘The Pirate Queen’ is incredibly special,” Singer tells Variety. “I’m especially proud that it’s for an immersive project. We started with a story we really believed in and wanted to bring it to life in a completely different way, something audiences could truly step inside and experience.”

A friend who went through the program before her told her to make the most of every opportunity. “So that’s what I intend to do! I’m really looking forward to meeting other filmmakers and finding ways to take over the world together,” she says.

Singer says this year is the first time she has really felt a scalable and sustainable future for immersive storytelling. “I’ve been genuinely encouraged by the level of distribution interest around ‘The Pirate Queen.’ It feels like there is a real appetite for immersive work now,” she says.

Liu sees the form as both an extension of filmmaking and something new. “It grows from cinematic language but it also asks the audience to participate differently. That changes the relationship between story and viewer,” she says. “We’re still discovering the language of immersive storytelling which is what makes this moment so exciting creatively.”

Singer’s background is in film and TV, and alongside new immersive work she is developing scripted projects. “I’ve always been drawn to stories about people who challenge expectations, whether they’ve been overlooked by history, underestimated by others, or simply refused to play by the rules,” she says. “Ultimately, I want to keep telling stories I really believe in and finding the most exciting ways to bring them to life.”
