Marvel Studios' existential superhero series "VisionQuest" has arrived on Disney+, and we've already been treated to four intriguing episodes that delve into the complex life of Vision, Paul Bettany's intelligent android and former card-carrying member of The Avengers.

The staggered storyline leading up to this show began with 2021's "WandaVision" and the 2024 follow-up, "Agatha All Along," with Marvel Studios proclaiming "VisionQuest" to be "the final vision of the groundbreaking trilogy." So, for those trying to catch up on current events in this trilogy of MCU shows starring Vision, and to avoid any lingering confusion, let’s take a step back to fill in the gaps.

And now, this isn't as simple as just "watch all the Marvel movies and shows in order," because that is a frankly ridiculous undertaking and entirely too much homework to do before watching a show. We're distilling it down to just what you need to know to understand VisionQuest.

Spoiler warning: It should go without saying, but there are spoilers for previous Marvel movies and shows in this article. You have been warned!

We'll go into some detail on all the connections below, but if you just want a list of the essential Marvel shows and movies to watch before VisionQuest, here it is.

Note that this is just the essentials. There are loads of small references to other movies and shows in the MCU, but they're just nods.

*This one is debatable. It continues Wanda's story from WandaVision, but it's not really essential for understanding the events of VisionQuest.

We kick things off with 2018's "Avengers: Infinity War," where the mighty Thanos murdered Vision by plucking out his golden, forehead-mounted Mind Stone for his Infinity Gauntlet. From that moment forward, Vision was dead, and Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) was cast into unfathomable grief and not-so-repressed anger.

From there, we pick up the story in the 2021 Disney+ series "WandaVision." Set weeks after "Avengers: Endgame," this show features two separate versions of Vision.

One was a new synthezoid version, Frankensteined together from the components of the old Vision by S.W.O.R.D., nicknamed White Vision. The other Vision is a supernatural manifestation, brought to life via Wanda Maximoff’s sorcery; he is known as Hex Vision.

So, which of these two Visions appears in "VisionQuest"? That's the fun (and confusing) part, because the answer is both of them. At the end of "WandaVision," Hex Vision restores the lost memories of White Vision, essentially merging two entities into one.

So, the Vision we see in "VisionQuest" is the physical body of White Vision, injected with thoughts and remembrances of the model that was magically resurrected by Wanda. Confused yet? Don't worry, it's going to get weirder.

In addition to the two versions of Vision from "WandaVision," numerous other AIs exist within Vision's skull and are all represented by human avatars acting as factions of his ravaged psyche.

Cast your mind all the way back to 2015's "Avengers: Age of Ultron," and you'll remember that Vision was conceived from a combination of the artificial brain of Ultron, the Mind Stone, and fragments of Tony Stark’s AI butler companion, J.A.R.V.I.S., who was named after the real Jarvis seen in the "Agent Carter" TV series.

J.A.R.V.I.S. appears in "VisionQuest" as his own unique entity, alongside another of Tony Stark's AI helpers, E.D.I.T.H., aka the AI in the smart glasses that Stark left to Peter Parker after his death. She shows up in "Spider-Man: Far From Home," which is a great movie but not an essential viewing if you're preparing for "VisionQuest."

Then let's toss in the fact that papa Ultron (James Spader) is buzzing around in Vision’s cranium, creating what’s been described as more or less an "Age of Ultron" and a "WandaVision" sequel at the same time. As it turns out, Vision did not destroy Ultron at the end of "Age of Ultron"; he copied his code and absorbed him, so now the rabid robot lives on in Vision’s brain.

The show’s narrative is centered around the complicated relationship between Vision and his son Tommy Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). Tommy was created by Wanda's Hex and should have disappeared when it collapsed, but both he and his brother Billy survived through magical shenanigans that are explained in 2024's "Agatha All Along."

Those two Maximoff boys, Tommy and Billy, both vanished from existence at the conclusion of "WandaVision." "Agatha All Along" exposed the truth that their consciousnesses entered the ether before expiring, only to reemerge into the souls of two teenage boys who had just perished, therefore returning them to life. Are you still with us? Good, just checking.

The finale of "Agatha All Along" hinted at the return of the estranged Tommy, and "VisionQuest" dives into that dangling plot point with relish!

Every show needs an antagonist, and the voices in Vision's head can't do all the work. "VisionQuest" has introduced a duo of villains for Vision to contend with. Neither of them has shown up in the MCU previously, though, so you don't need to do any research here.

With a massive bounty on his head after breaking free from S.W.O.R.D.'s control, White Vision must contend with a new villainous foe in the form of a mysterious mercenary named Paladin (Todd Stashwick).

This enigmatic Marvel Comics character was created by Jim Shooter and Carmine Infantino and was first seen prowling the pages of "Daredevil #150" back in 1978. He's basically a gun-for-hire in the Marvel universe, often hired to fight alongside or against various heroes depending on the story. We don't know much about his motivations in the show, but we'll learn more as it goes on.

"VisionQuest" also shines a spotlight on the bizarro character of Ultron's "bride," Jocasta, though the MCU version of this character diverges wildly from the comic book inspiration.

It's enough to drive one to madness! Between all the father-son dynamics dancing around the eight scheduled episodes, being hunted down by mercs, and his transcendent search for meaning, Vision and his saga are hopefully headed to a peaceful end.

Created by Terry Matalas ("Star Trek: Picard," "12 Monkeys") and airing two new chapters each Tuesday night on Disney+, VisionQuest is bolstered by a cast that includes Ruaridh Mollica, T'Nia Miller, Lauren Morais, Orla Brady, Diane Morgan, Polly Frame, Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer, Emily Hampshire, and James D’Arcy.

#599. America's largest budget airline reports 71% jump in airfare

Frontier Airlines reported a 71% increase in airfare in the third quarter as the country's largest budget airline tried to pass along an even bigger jump in jet fuel prices.

Frontier's fare revenue averaged $67.82 per passenger in the third quarter, compared with $39.74 last year. Including the budget airline's many fees, such as for checked and carry-on luggage, total revenue per passenger rose 30% on the year to $138.22.

Customers kept booking despite the higher prices. Frontier's passenger count rose 18% to more than 9.8 million people in the quarter. That's a difference of 1.5 million passengers from last year.

The company said demand remains strong, even at these higher prices, but Frontier still lost money as it took a $134 million charge tied to the return of some Airbus aircraft. Excluding that and other one-time charges, Frontier had an adjusted profit of $40 million.

Its posted a net loss of $104 million compared with a $77 million loss a year earlier. Its fuel bill soared 82% to $425 million.

Frontier forecast potential adjusted profit in the fourth quarter, saying it expects to post an adjusted loss of 15 cents per share to adjusted earnings of as much as 5 cents per share.

Carriers from Delta Air Lines to Frontier have said customers are mostly continuing to book flights despite higher fares, but that record jet fuel prices, their biggest cost after labor, are eroding profits.

Frontier had eclipsed Spirit Airlines as the biggest discount carrier in the country even before that airline collapsed in May.

#598. Is it legit? How to tell if that website or social media account is a scam

There is a 30 percent chance this article is fake.

It's not, of course. I am a real reporter. These are real sources. You can trust me.

According to a recent study from Pew Research, around one-third of recent web content is AI-generated. Around 10 percent of ".com" sites now have AI's fingerprints on them. Fake news sources peddling misinformation or propaganda (commonly referred to as "pink slime") have long outnumbered real news publishers — and are continuing to multiply with the help of AI.

Even legit websites and social platforms can steer you toward misinformation, scams, and other online dangers. A platform built to keep you hooked to an endless feed, fed by engagement and seeking to capture your attention, is a recipe for bots, phishing, and disinformation campaigns. Social media "experts" — sometimes entirely AI-generated people, other times real humans with ulterior motives — are building followings in the millions. In this increasingly confusing environment, here's how to get to the truth.

"High quality misinformation and deception were largely the domain of nation-states and well resourced groups," explained Donnie Hasseltine, chief information security officer at Arkstone Defense. Now, anyone can fake a site, build a bot, or amplify a misleading claim in an instant.

In addition to a decline in platform moderation, access to increasingly sophisticated AI models, mainly through open source markets, has completely changed how information is published, explained Zohaib Ahmed, CEO of deepfake detector Resemble.AI.

Likened to the "Wild West" by Ahmed, bad actors now have access to a host of AI models and tools without built-in safeguards to prove or disprove authenticity. They can avoid automatic detection built into mainstream models like Claude or ChatGPT, uploading troves of user and site data to build sophisticated spoofs without alerting developers.

The technology has generated a ballooning market for affordable "scam kits." Such kits cover "everything from advertising to writing blog posts and content on social media, to how features are being built in the product, how video calls are being done and how images are being uploaded onto social media platforms," Ahmed said. With a few hundred dollars, scammers can spoof entire sites, make convincing log-in portals, and build natural-looking engagement that makes it feel more real.

It's not just relegated to pink slime, either. You may encounter "url hijackers" or "typosquatting" for instance. These webpages closely mimic URLs for reputable sites — including news sites like "abcnews.com.co" or known organizations like FIFA — banking on users not looking too close. Others may spoof sites where it's common to exchange money or place bets. These domains may siphon off your personal information or try to steal your money outright.

The same happens on social media sites and chatrooms: X accounts meant to look like real people, dodgy TikTok Shop links that take users off site, suspicious links dropped in gaming chats by players you thought were your friends.

"The traditional signals of authenticity are fading," explained Eyal Elazar, head of market intelligence for e-commerce security business Riskified. "Only a few years ago, verifying something online relied on recognizable visual or contextual cues: a weirdly spelled URL, pixelated image artifacts, a robotic cadence in a video, or the sheer logistical effort required to pull off a coordinated hoax. Today, AI can effortlessly clean up misspelled URLs, blurry images, and stiff video voices."

Because users are up against a modern world of AI-powered websites and bot accounts, they also need new advice for scouring through the muck.

The OG way to ensure you're on a legit site still works and is very simple: Check the URL.

First, look for the padlock icon or other indicator the browser has verified your connection. For Google Chrome users, select the menu icon to the left of the URL. You should see "Connection is secure."

Second, look for "https://" not "http://". The "s" designation means a site has been authenticated.

These security components are still essential components of the internet, explained Ron Kerbs, CEO of AI fraud prevention company Kidas.

Third, double-check the URL's spelling, says Ahmed. Keep an eye out for symbols in the place of letters and non-English characters masquerading as the English alphabet. Hover over a URL to see the full text.

If you're still unsure, search the URL on Google. You can also cross-reference URLs on Google's site status page or use an online URL scanning tool, Ahmed recommends.  The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Many mainstream browsers now include built-in safety checks that flag when a website doesn't meet these security parameters. Pay attention to them, and only follow through on visiting a site if you know its origins.

But bear in mind that social media accounts do not play by these rules, experts warn.

To verify an account is legit, start with the platform's own verification tools, like the classic check mark. Be sure to click through to the profile itself, not just how it appears on your feed. Many platforms allow custom characters in display names, which help users fake verified check marks on first glance. Other platforms, like X, let users buy verification, so use additional means to confirm those accounts.

Be on alert for AI-generated influencer content, too. Look for AI content labels in captions, comments, and on profiles. Use the tips below to see if they've skirted detection (many do).

A site or account may seem legit on the surface, but its content could be far from it. Basic security measures aren't prevention for misinformation or manipulative content posted to verified platforms, experts say.

"You close the door, someone gets in through the window," Kerbs said. Users should use multiple layers additional methods beyond URL scanning to verify that what they're looking at is real.

Traditional recommendations for vetting news sources, for example, include the SIFT method. It's an oft-referred to media literacy skill designed by misinformation researcher Mike Caufield and stands for:

Other news literacy groups, like the News Literacy Project, suggest a strategy of "zoning," or  categorizing content, including websites and social media accounts, by their purpose.

"Identify the type of information you are looking at and determine its purpose. Is it news that’s meant to inform you? Or an opinion that’s trying to persuade you? Or is it a paid ad that’s encouraging you to buy something?" said Chuck Salter, president and CEO of the News Literacy Project. Salter recommends online users zone first before making judgements about trust. "You need to understand the main intent."

Salter also recommends a fact-checking concept called "lateral reading," in which you verify a source by searching what others are saying about it.

This can be used to fact check social media accounts, too. Before resharing, check the algorithm. How do others feel about this page?

Methods like SIFT and zoning are fairly simple and very effective ways to spot misinformation. But we're up against platforms actively working to steal our attention span and keep us glued to their platforms. We are urged to use integrated generative AI tools intended to reduce friction, but which can reduce users' critical thinking, experts say. Young people are at particular risk, Salter explained, and often fail to properly "zone" content without help.

We may need to simplify our toolkit even further.

For one, never trust a screenshot, said Roei Sherman, senior director of research at cloud security firm Mitiga. A common way to spread misinformation, faked screenshots feed off of the attention economy: Get enough people to share the eye-grabbing headline or quote, and you'll convince a good amount of people it's true, especially if a generally reliable source is slapped on top.

Second rule of thumb: If a post feels like rage bait, it's probably rage bait. Scammers and propagandists stoke emotional responses to get your clicks, Rubinson explains. Try not to engage.

And lastly, if an account is asking you to leave the platform you're on, exercise caution. Fake accounts often steer users off of moderated platforms toward other websites with looser content guidelines or toward completely unregulated areas of the internet. It's why many social media giants, like TikTok, have specific rules against the promotion of off-platform sites.

If it's best to check a claim with multiple sources, it's even better to check the claim with an authority that makes fact-checking its job. Long before AI, these sites existed as nonpartisan sources for political claims. Now, they've expanded to cover just about anything going viral.

NewsGuard AI False Claims Monitor and Reality Check newsletter

Some cybersecurity experts recommend browser extensions that can automatically scan a page for AI-generated content and give an assessment of its trustworthiness. These are a good starting point, but like most detector tech, are not infallible, experts like Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN, warn.

Resemble.AI Deepfake Detector: Scans all images, video, and audio and returns a verdict on whether or not AI was used. A free account includes four website scans per day.

NewsGuard: Provides a trust and reliability rating for news sites, based on nonpartisan criteria.

McAfee Web Advisor: The free version of the cybersecurity's fraud tool, Web Advisor scans for malicious sites, including hidden adware, spyware, and phishing scams.

This rainbow-hued rocky plain looks like the landscape of an alien world. And, it turns out, it is.

In this image, we can see an ancient, rocky hill on Mars. In the Red Planet's Southern Highlands, this alien terrain is chock-full of minerals, which we can see clearly defined in this color-enhanced view of the region.

This image was snapped by the HiRISE camera aboard NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), which has been studying the planet's surface, atmosphere and climate since arriving in Martian orbit in March 2006.

But this isn't exactly what the surface of the planet would look like through our eyes; the image is color-enhanced. Why would scientists take a natural-color image and turn it rainbow? Doing so enhances the slight color differences in these rocks, allowing researchers to pick out the different minerals.

As pointed to above, enhancing colors in scientific images can be an incredibly useful tool for exploration.

For instance, in this image, the blue- and green-toned rocks could be full of minerals like pyroxenes and olivine, according to scientists analyzing the image. And they think that the yellow, orange and red patches may contain minerals formed by past interactions with liquid water.

By exploring the mineral content of rocks like this, researchers can peel back the layers of history within the Martian bedrock. The discovery of certain minerals, for example, can show that water flowed on Mars long ago, pointing to potentially habitable conditions.

So, as we can see, this striking rainbow image isn't just a beautiful landscape; it's also hiding serious clues to Mars' history.

#596. Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half

The liver may hold an unexpected key to fighting two of the most serious diseases associated with aging: Alzheimer's disease and heart disease. Scientists have discovered that restoring the function of aging liver cells can dramatically reduce harmful substances in the bloodstream, raising the possibility of treating diseases that affect organs far beyond the liver itself.

In a new study involving older rats, researchers at the Keck School of Medicine of USC found that an experimental drug called cinaciguat reversed important signs of aging in specialized liver cells. After just two weeks of treatment, levels of amyloid beta, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease, dropped by half. Levels of LDL, commonly called bad cholesterol, also returned to those seen in younger animals.

The findings, published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry, also revealed a previously unknown way that liver cells communicate with one another. This discovery could help scientists develop treatments that restore the liver's ability to remove potentially harmful substances from the blood, possibly reducing the risk of Alzheimer's disease and atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty deposits accumulate inside arteries.

Why the Liver Could Be Important for Alzheimer's

Although Alzheimer's primarily affects the brain, scientists are increasingly interested in how other organs might influence the disease. The liver plays a central role in filtering the blood and removing unwanted compounds, including substances that may contribute to disease when they accumulate.

The USC findings suggest that restoring this natural cleaning process could offer a different approach to preventing certain age-related illnesses. However, the results have so far been demonstrated only in rats, and additional studies are needed to establish whether the same benefits occur in humans.

"We need to do further translational work to see whether our findings might point to new therapies," said corresponding author Laurie DeLeve, MD, PhD, professor and vice chair for scientific affairs in the USC Department of Medicine. "We're hopeful, though, because the findings line up with a lot of epidemiological results showing age as a major risk factor for Alzheimer's and atherosclerosis, and liver damage as a risk factor for Alzheimer's."

Targeting the liver could be particularly valuable in Alzheimer's research, where efforts to develop treatments acting directly in the brain have faced an estimated 98% failure rate in clinical trials. One major obstacle is the blood-brain barrier, a protective system that limits which substances can enter the brain from the bloodstream. While this barrier helps shield the brain from harmful compounds, it also makes delivering certain medications extremely difficult.

"If we're right that the liver is impactful, what do we do about that?" said first author Sam de Leve, MA, a USC lab technician and child of Laurie DeLeve. "Rather than trying to get a drug through the blood-brain barrier, which is obnoxiously difficult, we could direct drugs to the liver, an organ where there might be more therapeutic impact and certainly an easier job of drug delivery."

Scientists Restore the Aging Liver's Natural Filters

To understand how liver aging affects the bloodstream, the researchers focused on a relatively understudied group of cells known as liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs).

These cells form the lining of tiny blood vessels inside the liver. Unlike most blood vessel walls, they contain numerous microscopic openings that function somewhat like the holes in a sieve. These openings allow larger molecules circulating in the blood to reach neighboring cells called hepatocytes, which carry out much of the liver's work processing and removing substances from the body.

As the liver ages, the openings in LSECs gradually become smaller or disappear. This makes it harder for certain large molecules to reach the cells responsible for clearing them, allowing more of these substances to remain in circulation.

One substance affected by this change is amyloid beta. This protein is especially important in Alzheimer's research because it can accumulate in the brain and form plaques, one of the disease's defining features.

Previous observations showed that the liver becomes less effective at removing amyloid beta as it ages. The researchers suspected that the gradual closing of the openings in LSECs might help explain why more of the protein remains in the bloodstream of older animals.

To investigate, they administered cinaciguat to aged rats for two weeks. They then compared the treated animals with two untreated groups, one consisting of older rats and the other of younger rats.

The results were striking. Cinaciguat restored the structure and function of the aging LSECs, reopening their microscopic pores and improving their ability to help clear substances from the blood. Amyloid beta concentrations fell by approximately 50%, reaching levels comparable to those in young rats. The untreated older animals showed no similar improvement.

The researchers also measured low-density lipoproteins (LDL), often referred to as "bad" cholesterol because elevated levels contribute to fatty deposits inside arteries. Over time, these deposits can restrict blood flow and increase the risk of heart disease.

Initially, LDL was included as a comparison measure rather than a substance expected to respond to treatment. Unlike larger molecules, LDL particles are small enough to leave the bloodstream without passing through the microscopic openings in LSECs. The scientists therefore expected cinaciguat to have little or no effect on LDL levels.

Instead, they discovered that LDL concentrations in treated older rats also fell to levels observed in young animals.

"We said, 'Wait, why did that go down? Clearly, there's more to this story,'" Sam de Leve said.

The unexpected finding suggested that the drug was doing more than simply reopening the liver's aging filters. It appeared to be restoring another important aspect of liver function.

Because previous research had shown that hepatocytes function better when LSECs are present, the team began examining how these two types of cells communicate.

Their investigation uncovered a previously unknown sequence of biochemical signals that helps coordinate the liver's ability to remove substances from the bloodstream.

A Hidden Communication Pathway Between Liver Cells

The researchers found that cinaciguat activates an enzyme called soluble guanylate cyclase inside LSECs. This triggers the cells to release a growth factor known as HB-EGF, which sends a signal to nearby hepatocytes.

In response, hepatocytes alter their surfaces in ways that allow them to capture more LDL and amyloid beta from the blood. This helps explain why the treatment reduced both substances, even though they do not rely on the same filtering mechanism.

Normally, aging interferes with the ability of LSECs to release HB-EGF. Cinaciguat restored this signaling process, allowing the liver cells to communicate more effectively and supporting the removal of substances that otherwise tend to accumulate with age.

The discovery identifies a potential new target for future drugs. Rather than focusing exclusively on the physical openings in LSECs, researchers may be able to develop therapies that restore the chemical signals responsible for helping the liver work efficiently.

Could Liver Rejuvenation Help Prevent Alzheimer's and Heart Disease?

According to the researchers, this is the first study to demonstrate that a drug can fully restore the structure and function of aging LSECs, including their ability to support the clearance of substances from the bloodstream.

It is also the first to show that a treatment directed at the liver can bring age-related elevations in circulating amyloid beta and LDL back to youthful levels.

These findings raise the possibility that cinaciguat, similar medications, or treatments targeting HB-EGF could eventually be used to counteract certain effects of liver aging. If those changes translate into meaningful protection against disease, they could provide new strategies for preventing Alzheimer's and cardiovascular problems.

For now, however, the findings represent an early step. Lowering amyloid beta in the bloodstream does not necessarily mean that amyloid plaques in the brain will decrease or that Alzheimer's disease can be prevented.

The researchers plan to continue studying cinaciguat in rats to determine whether its effects on amyloid beta actually translate into measurable protection against Alzheimer's disease.

They also hope the findings will encourage scientists studying other conditions, particularly atherosclerosis, to investigate how restoring liver function might influence disease development.

"We hope that people who are in fields like atherosclerosis research read this, and want to grab the idea for themselves," Sam de Leve said. "There are six different ways someone could go with this, and we can't do them all. So please, scoop us. We'd love it."

Additional researchers involved in the study include Xiangdong Wang, Helia Alavifard and Lily Dara, all affiliated with the Keck School of Medicine of USC.

The research received federal funding from the National Institutes of Health [R56AG071480, 5R01DK100580].

On Nov. 2, 2000, the International Space Station welcomed its first long-term residents.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 2, 2000, the International Space Station welcomed its first long-term residents: NASA astronaut Bill Shepherd and two Russian cosmonauts, Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev. The mission was called Expedition 1.

Before this expedition, NASA had launched five, one-week-long Space Shuttle missions to help build the space station and bring up supplies. But this time, the crew would be staying for four and a half months, and they weren't taking the shuttle. Instead, they took a Russian Soyuz spacecraft, and this was the first Soyuz to ever dock at the space station.

During their stay at the space station, they unpacked supplies and installed new equipment, including the first solar arrays. They left on the space shuttle Discovery, which brought up the Expedition 2 crew that would take their place.

As of today, there has been a continuous astronaut presence in space aboard the International Space Station for 26 years. For all of these years, not a day has gone by without someone living in space, orbiting our planet from aboard the space station.

While the ISS was not the first space station, it has been the longest-running space statin by far. This first crew were pioneers, showing how humans could actually live and work aboard this station. This exploratory mission proved that the station could successfully support astronaut crews.

Since this mission 26 years ago, there have been literally hundreds of astronauts from around the world who have flown to and lived aboard the ISS. While NASA has stated that the station might be decommissioned in the coming years, these accomplishments will remain forever in spaceflight history.

#593. Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists

Scientists have proposed a surprising new explanation for why the universe exists, and it centers on a mysterious particle that physicists have largely overlooked for decades. Their theory suggests this forgotten particle may have played a crucial role in shaping the early cosmos and allowing matter to survive after the Big Bang.

The research addresses one of the most fundamental mysteries in physics: why does the universe contain matter instead of nothing at all? Scientists believe matter and antimatter were produced in nearly equal amounts in the early universe. When these opposites encounter one another, they annihilate and release energy. If they had existed in perfectly equal quantities, virtually all matter could have disappeared, leaving no material to form stars, planets, or life.

Now, researchers from the University of Southampton and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur believe they may have found an important piece of the puzzle. Their explanation involves a little-understood relative of the neutrino, an extremely lightweight particle that rarely interacts with ordinary matter.

A Forgotten Particle With a Powerful Role in the Early Universe

The team focused on a type of particle known as a 'decoupled' heavy neutrino. Unlike ordinary neutrinos, this hypothetical heavier relative has generally been considered too weakly connected to other particles to significantly influence the universe.

However, the researchers found that its unusually long lifetime could have made it far more important than previously thought. According to their calculations, the particle may have survived long enough to temporarily dominate the universe's energy density as the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang.

That brief period of dominance could have altered how the early universe evolved, influencing the conditions that ultimately allowed matter to outnumber antimatter.

Dr. Rishav Roshan of the University of Southampton, an author of the study, explained:

"This decoupled heavy neutrino has long been dismissed as an irrelevant background detail in particle physics.

"However, it decays incredibly slowly. As the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang, the particle lived long enough that it temporarily took over the energy density of the universe and triggered a matter-dominated period."

The findings were published in Physical Review Letters, a scientific journal of the American Physical Society.

How a Heavy Neutrino Could Explain Why Matter Survived

Previous attempts to explain why matter prevailed over antimatter generally left out the decoupled heavy neutrino. Because it interacts so weakly with other particles, scientists assumed it would have little influence on the processes responsible for creating the imbalance.

The new research challenges that assumption. The team found that even a particle with extremely weak interactions could indirectly affect the conditions under which matter gained its crucial advantage.

This imbalance, known as matter and antimatter asymmetry, is essential to understanding our existence. For reasons physicists are still trying to explain, the early universe ended up with slightly more matter than antimatter. That small difference allowed some matter to remain after most particles and their antiparticles annihilated one another.

"The fact that we are here at all proves that an asymmetry between matter and antimatter occurred," added Dr. Roshan.

"The decoupled neutrino shifted the temperature in the early universe at which fundamental particles - like electrons and other leptons - interacted with their anti-particles with the help of Standard Model Higgs boson.

"This temperature acts like a switch that shapes how the matter-antimatter imbalance was built up."

The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle associated with the mechanism that gives many elementary particles their mass. In the researchers' proposed scenario, the heavy neutrino changed the temperature conditions governing important particle interactions involving the Higgs boson.

By shifting when these interactions occurred, the particle could have influenced how the imbalance between matter and antimatter developed. In other words, something long considered insignificant may have helped determine why the universe contains matter at all.

Ancient Gravitational Waves Could Reveal the Answer

The theory could also have important implications for understanding how the universe expanded in its earliest stages.

Study co-author Dr. Sudipta Show of the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said the findings suggest that the forgotten particle may have dramatically altered the expansion history of the young cosmos.

He added: "It offers us a new explanation for how matter won.

"The dramatic shift in the early expansion of the cosmos leaves distinct but detectable imprints of changes, for example on primordial gravitational waves.

"These gravitational wave signatures open up new avenues for us to unravel the evolution of the early universe after the Big Bang."

Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of space and time. Scientists believe processes in the extremely early universe may have generated primordial gravitational waves that carry information about conditions from that distant era.

According to the new theory, the temporary dominance of the heavy neutrino could have left recognizable signatures in those ancient signals. Detecting such patterns could eventually provide a way to investigate whether the proposed particle really influenced the universe's earliest evolution.

For now, the explanation remains theoretical. But it offers physicists a new possibility for solving one of cosmology's deepest mysteries: how matter survived when its encounter with antimatter could have left the universe almost entirely empty.

The findings are another clue towards understanding the origins of 3I/ATLAS and the planet-forming conditions around other stars.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), scientists have found that the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS was built from tiny grains of ice mixed with dust that are quite different from the solar system’s comets.

These ice grains do, however, bear striking similarities to some icy bodies located at the edge of the solar system, beyond the orbit of Neptune, so-called trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs).

3I/ATLAS was discovered entering the solar system in the summer of 2025. It was only the third object found entering the solar system from farther afield in the Milky Way after 1I/'Oumuamua, seen in 2017, and 2I/Borisov, detected in 2019. This meant the interstellar comet offered a rare chance to glimpse the conditions under which such bodies form in other star systems. Thus, the JWST was quickly on the trail of 3I/ATLAS.

"We designed [JWST] to be ready the moment an active interstellar comet was found and to follow it over time," Martin Cordiner of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and the Catholic University of America said in a statement.

Cordiner leads the JWST program to study objects such as 3I/ATLAS, and he is a co-author on a new research paper describing some of the findings.

Researchers know that 3I/ATLAS wasn't born in the solar system, but nobody knows around which star 3I/ATLAS formed. What scientists are more sure of is the fact that this interstellar comet was produced within a planet-forming disk of gas and dust around a young star, possibly as long ago as 10 to 12 billion years. That's over twice the age of our solar system. It was then ejected from its home system somehow and left to wander interstellar space before encountering our solar system.

Like the familiar comets in our solar system, 3I/ATLAS is composed of grains of ice less than a micron – a millionth of a meter – in size. When the surface of the comet is warmed by the sun, gas erupts outwards, carrying ice grains into the cloud of ice and dust surrounding the comet, its coma, and its tail, where JWST can detect them.

When viewed spectroscopically, the water-ice in comets native to our solar system creates a strong absorption line in a comet’s spectrum at a wavelength of three microns, as well as less-prominent absorption lines at 1.5 and two microns.

Yet when the JWST’s Near-Infrared spectrograph (NIRSpec) instrument viewed 3I/ATLAS three times between August 2025, before its closest approach to the sun, and after closest approach in April 2026, scientists found the 1.5- and two micron absorption lines were missing, though the three-micron line remained strong.

"That combination was a puzzle," research lead author Silvia Protopapa of the South-west Research Institute said. "The strong three-micron band points to water-ice in the coma, but the weak or absent shorter-wavelength bands suggest the ice is not in the form we usually see in solar system comets."

Whenever presented with an unusual observational signature such the JWST delievered for 3I/ATLAS researchers turn to modeling to find the physical characteristics that best fit the spectrum. The modeling suggested to Protopapa’s team that 3I/ATLAS was composed of sub-micron grains of dirty water-ice, rich in dust. In comparison, the grains from the solar system’s indigenous comets are much cleaner, with almost pure water-ice relatively uncontaminated by dust."What seems to set [3I/ATLAS’ grains] apart is how much dust is mixed into the ice," said Protopapa. "Those grains hold clues to the conditions where the comet was born."

Comets are made of primordial material found in the planet-forming disk of gas and dust that surrounds a young star, and therefore the composition of comets can provide a window into the conditions in which planets form.

Whereas solar system comets tell us about the birth of Earth, an interstellar comet can tell us about conditions in which planets formed around another star, and how similar or dissimilar those conditions were to the birth of the solar system.

Yet comets are not the only icy remnants that date back to such primordial times. There are various families of bodies in the outer solar system, and 3I/ATLAS’ spectrum bears a resemblance to the spectrum of some medium-sized TNOs that are rich in carbon-dioxide ice and organic compounds (organic meaning containing carbon atoms). Indeed, in a separate 2025 study led by Cordiner, the JWST found 3I/ATLAS to have one of the greatest abundances of carbon dioxide ever seen in a comet.

TNOs are sizable bodies that are located far beyond the orbit of Neptune, The TNOs in question would have formed in a different part of the Sun’s protoplanetary disk than most comets and their composition reflects that.

On the other hand, the results imply that 3I/ATLAS was formed around its star of origin from similar icy material to that which produced some of the TNOs in our solar system, showing that the building blocks of planets around other stars share a common range of properties with the building blocks that formed our solar system. Indeed, 3I/ATLAS could even be a fragment of a TNO-like body that was shattered in a collision.

"At first glance, 3I/ATLAS looks different from the icy comets we know," said Protopapa. "But when we placed it alongside distant icy worlds in our own solar system, it no longer looked out of place. "This suggests that the icy building block of planets, here and around other stars, may share ice in the form of tiny, micron-scale grains, ranging from relatively pure ice to ice mixed with dust, with 3I/ATLAS toward the dusty end."

What this tells us is that these sub-micron-sized icy grains must form first in planet-forming disks, to then be incorporated into large bodies such as comets and protoplanets.

The team's findings were published on Monday (Oct. 26) in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#591. NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past

NASA's Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have uncovered surprising clues about the earliest days of our solar system by examining some of the smallest and faintest objects ever observed beyond Neptune. The findings challenge expectations about how planets form and suggest that these distant, icy bodies have preserved evidence of their origins for billions of years.

For the first time, astronomers combined observations from Hubble and Webb to investigate trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs), tiny bodies that travel around the Sun far beyond Neptune's orbit. Researchers discovered 27 previously unknown objects, but their findings revealed an unexpected puzzle. There were fewer small objects than some theories predicted, and their colors closely resembled those of much larger objects in the same distant regions.

These frozen remnants offer a rare opportunity to study the materials that eventually became planets. Most are extraordinarily difficult to detect, shining more than 100 million times more faintly than objects visible to the naked eye. Two related studies published in The Astronomical Journal examined the newly identified objects to learn more about their sizes, compositions, and ancient history.

Ancient Building Blocks of the Solar System

Scientists believe planets began forming when tiny particles of dust and pebbles orbiting the young Sun gradually accumulated into larger bodies. Over time, these materials formed objects roughly the size of cities, known as "planetesimals." These early building blocks eventually combined to create the planets we see today.

However, that final stage of growth did not occur for many objects beyond Neptune. Instead of developing into full-sized planets, countless smaller bodies remained, preserving evidence of the solar system's earliest period of formation.

To investigate these distant survivors, research teams led by PhD candidates at the University of Victoria in Canada, working under the guidance of the National Research Council of Canada, and Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff conducted the deepest survey of trans-Neptunian objects to date. Both space telescopes observed the same region of sky simultaneously, with Hubble collecting visible light and Webb capturing infrared light.

By combining these observations, astronomers could examine the objects' colors, estimate their sizes, and determine how they orbit the Sun. Their colors are especially valuable because they provide clues about the chemical makeup of their surfaces, much like fingerprints that reveal an object's identity and history.

The researchers focused on two distinct populations of trans-Neptunian objects, known as dynamically "cold" and dynamically "hot" TNOs. These descriptions refer to their orbital behavior rather than their temperatures.

Cold objects have largely remained in the regions where they originally formed. They follow relatively circular paths around the Sun and stay close to the plane in which most of the solar system's planets orbit.

Hot objects have experienced a much more turbulent history. They originally formed between the present-day orbits of Uranus and Neptune but were scattered outward as the giant planets shifted positions early in the solar system's development. Their current orbits are much more elongated, and they travel above and below the solar system's main orbital plane.

Despite these dramatically different histories, the two populations revealed an unexpected similarity. Even the smallest objects appear to have retained surface characteristics resembling those of their larger counterparts.

Tiny Worlds Preserve Their Ancient Origins

Before the observations, scientists suspected that smaller TNOs would show clear evidence of repeated collisions over billions of years. Impacts could have fractured the objects and exposed fresh material, potentially changing their surface compositions and colors.

Instead, the newly discovered objects displayed the same general color relationships seen among larger TNOs. This suggests that collisions may have altered their surfaces much less than expected.

One possibility is that these objects have experienced fewer impacts than astronomers previously assumed. Another is that their surfaces somehow retain their original compositions even after collisions. Researchers have not yet determined which explanation is correct.

"You could imagine a scenario where getting knocked around and fragmented would change the surface composition, and then you would see a different surface color for tiny TNOs compared to their larger siblings. So it's really fascinating to see that the smallest objects are somehow 'remembering' and preserving the history of how they were made," said Northern Arizona University PhD candidate Anastasia Morgan, who led the study of color and composition.

"These dynamically 'hot' TNOs retain a signature of where they were born, even though they've been orbitally scrambled since then," said co-author David Trilling of Northern Arizona University.

The observations indicate that both hot and cold TNOs have maintained color patterns linked to their formation, with surprisingly little apparent change since the solar system's beginnings. These ancient objects may therefore preserve important information about the environments in which they first took shape.

Webb Finds Fewer Tiny Worlds Than Expected

The James Webb Space Telescope also provided another important piece of the puzzle. Its observations allowed scientists to examine how many objects exist at different sizes, revealing an unexpected resemblance between the two populations.

Although hot and cold TNOs formed in different parts of the early solar system, their overall size distributions were remarkably alike. This suggests that the processes responsible for creating planetesimals may have operated in much the same way across different environments.

"It's very interesting that the process of planetesimal formation ends up producing the same distribution of sizes for both cold and hot populations, despite forming in different regions of the early solar system. The process seems to be insensitive to disk conditions, producing similar planetesimal sizes whether the disk is hot or cold, and dense or fluffy," said University of Victoria PhD candidate Marielle Eduardo, who led the study on size distribution.

The researchers also identified a surprising shortage of very small TNOs compared with predictions from some existing planet formation models. Understanding why fewer objects were detected could help scientists refine their explanations of how the solar system's original building blocks developed.

Webb's extraordinary sensitivity made it possible to discover 27 exceptionally faint objects. One was so dim that detecting it would be comparable to standing on Earth and spotting a small swarm of fireflies on the Moon.

The smallest object measured just 3 miles (5 kilometers) across, making it approximately five times smaller than the objects detectable with even the most sensitive telescopes on the ground.

Hubble and Webb Reveal New Clues to Planet Formation

These discoveries depended on the complementary capabilities of NASA's two powerful space observatories. Hubble's ability to detect visible light and Webb's sensitivity to infrared light gave scientists a more complete picture of the distant objects than either telescope could have provided independently.

Together, the telescopes have opened a new window into a largely unexplored population of ancient solar system remnants. Their surprising similarities, preserved surface characteristics, and unexpected numbers offer important clues about the processes that shaped the planets billions of years ago.

Materials provided by NASA. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#589. Ford reports mixed third-quarter results, says 2027 earnings will be in line with this year

DETROIT — Ford Motor expects earnings next year will be roughly in line with the automaker's anticipated results this year, the company said Wednesday as it reported mixed results for the third quarter.

The Detroit automaker beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations but slightly missed revenue estimates. The company has been working to stabilize production of its F-Series pickup trucks after dealing with supplier issues for much of the past year.

"This quarter's results reflect deliberate actions to improve profitability and deliver consistent financial returns," Ford CFO Sherry House told reporters during a call Wednesday.

Ford reported third-quarter adjusted free cash flow of $4.7 billion, roughly $2 billion higher than what analysts were anticipating, according to StreetAccount.

Here's how Ford performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:

The Detroit automaker also narrowed its 2026 guidance to adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $10.5 billion and $11 billion, compared with a previous outlook of $10 billion to $11 billion. Ford maintained its adjusted free cash flow guidance for this year of between $6 billion and $7 billion.

House said the company expects 2027 earnings to be roughly in line with this year's results, citing several offsetting factors in production issues this year as well as rising commodity costs.

House noted a $1.3 billion tariff refund during the first quarter of this year was largely offset by additional costs from alternative aluminum sourcing that the company does not expect to have next year, leveling out the year-over-year comparison.

She also said production of its F-Series Super Duty trucks in Canada in 2027 will make up for lost production it's expecting at its F-150 factories to retool for new models.

"Next year will be the third year on our journey of increasing and improving our warranty and material cost savings, and that's getting extended to structural costs throughout the company as well in terms of savings," House said.

Ford CEO Jim Farley called 2027 a "foundational year" for the company on its way to a previously announced target of an 8% adjusted EBIT margin by 2029. The company reported a 5.4% margin during the third quarter.

Ahead of the results, Wall Street analysts were mixed about whether Ford would be able to maintain profits in 2027.

The company has multiple efforts that will add to costs next year: It's rolling out several new or redesigned models, including its next-generation EV and Canada-produced pickups, and is enhancing its energy business that it announced earlier this year.

The missed revenue for the third quarter was a result of each of the automaker's main business units – which are broken into Blue traditional operations, Pro fleet and Model e electric vehicle segments – underperforming compared with Wall Street's expectations, according to StreetAccount.

As part of its modified guidance, Ford said it now expects pre-tax earnings of its Ford Blue unit to be $5.5 billion, which is at the high end of a previous guidance.

It's also anticipating EBIT of about $7 billion for the year for Ford Pro and Ford Model e losses of about $4 billion. Its Ford Credit unit is expected to record about $2.8 billion in EBIT for 2026.

Ford's overall revenue, which includes its credit segment, was off roughly 2% compared with the third quarter of last year, to $49.5 billion.

Its net income also was off $400 million from a year earlier to $2 billion, while adjusted earnings before interest and taxes were up slightly year-over-year to $2.7 billion.

Ford's 2025 third-quarter results included $47.19 billion in automotive revenue, net income of $2.4 billion and earnings per share of 45 cents adjusted.

#588. Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO) lens review — how good is this budget lens for astrophotography?

The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO) is an impressive lens for the price and certainly won’t break the bank. Image quality is impressive but imperfect, yet it's still an attractive lens.

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

Budget primes can be, surprisingly, excellent choices for photographers shooting all subjects. It’s all too easy to get carried away with the best specs, such as a large maximum aperture and impressive optical design often seen in more expensive options. But affordable lenses like the Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II FE (APO) have the potential to impress and delight in equal measure.

The 35mm f/1.8 is a compact and lightweight lens offering a reasonably fast maximum aperture, making it a prime candidate for astrophotography. It’s also the same size and almost the same weight as the Viltrox AF 55mm f/1.8 FE (APO), another lens that could potentially grace your camera bag.

With a highly attractive price tag of just $399 / £385, and mount options for Nikon Z and Sony FE, many astrophotographers will be wondering if this is a lens worth considering. It features 13 elements in 10 groups, as well as featuring an apochromatic (APO) design for reducing chromatic aberration as much as possible. As much as possible is key here because not all lenses are as successful as the manufacturer claims, although that’s not a comment on the 35mm f/1.8. Read on to discover if this could be one of the best lenses for astrophotography.

For a budget lens, the 35mm f/1.8 produces great, yet not perfect, image quality. On the plus side, images are nice and sharp, particularly in the centre, even when shooting wide open at f/1.8. At this aperture setting, though, there is some astigmatism at the left edges of the frame. This is where stars appear as crosses. This is a surprise since it’s an APO lens, and, equally surprising, it’s isolated, but it is something you have to consider.

You do have to zoom into the image to see it, so it may not be a dealbreaker. Photos shot at f/1.8 are sharpest in the centre, with some fall-off towards the edges, with the corners exhibiting the least sharpness. There’s also the strongest vignetting at f/1.8. At the time of writing, there’s no Adobe Lightroom lens profile for the lens, but you can manually remove the vignetting and even create a preset of your own.

The vignette disappears as soon as f/4, with a gradual increase in sharpness across the frame between f/2.8 and f/5.6. f/8 and f/11 appear identical in terms of sharpness and occupy the sweet spot, while diffraction is clearly at work when you stop down to f/16. In reality, it’s unlikely you’d shoot beyond f/11 with this lens, even if you were shooting landscapes.

Overall, image quality is impressive despite not being perfect and stopping down to f/2.8 when shooting astro does provide greater clarity across the frame. This is, as you know, at the expense of having to shoot at a slightly higher ISO setting to compensate.

While f/1.8 lenses may not have the speed and light-gathering capabilities of faster f/1.4 and f/1.2 lenses, they’re considerably smaller and lighter. The lens only has a 58mm filter thread, so if you use any night filters, they will be at the less expensive end of the price scale.

For some photographers, the slight speed reduction of f/1.8 is a worthy compromise, and at 3.33 x 4.37 in / 69 x 76 mm with a weight of 12.52 oz / 355 g, the 35mm f/1.8 is beautifully compact and balances well with camera bodies.

Build quality is excellent, and it’s fair to say the lens belies its budget price tag. The metal build alongside the manual aperture ring gives the 35mm f/1.8 a much more premium look and feel.

The aperture ring can also be set to A for in-body aperture adjustments, as well as offering the ability to switch the aperture click on and off. The latter is most popular with videographers. There’s also a customizable Fn button on the side.

The lens is weather-sealed against light rain and dust, with a rubber gasket on the lens mount. The front element also features a water and smudge-resistant coating, which is certainly useful for outdoor photography. Plus, there’s a minimum focusing distance of just 13.4 in / 34 cm, which is useful for daylight photography but of no consequence for astrophotography.

The 35mm f/1.8 is made up of 13 elements in 10 groups, and as previously mentioned, features an APO design, which is intended to eliminate chromatic aberration in high-contrast scenes.

The elements include two extra-low dispersion (ED), three high refractive index (HR) and one ultra aspherical (UA). The UA lens is claimed to be Viltrox’s LAB Series quality, which matches the Viltrox flagship line-up.

When it comes to features, prime lenses are always pretty basic, with few features to shout about. The 35mm f/1.8 is certainly no exception, but its build quality and overall design hold up alongside its image quality and reasonably fast maximum aperture. It does, however, have a few points worth mentioning.

One feature that many Viltrox lenses have, including the 35mm f/1.8, is a USB-C Port on the lens mount. This allows you to use a smartphone app or a desktop app to quickly and easily update firmware. This is so much easier than having to download a file to your memory card and installing lens updates via the camera, which is how most native lenses have to be updated.

The manual aperture ring features click and clickless operation via a switch on the side, so you can easily see what aperture you’re using at a glance. The focusing ring is smooth and offers comfortable resistance, making manual focus a breeze. It’s also wide enough to rotate using gloves, although, being a compact lens, it’s narrower than what you’d expect on a larger and faster prime lens.

Autofocus (AF) is reasonably fast and silent, being powered by an stepping motor (STM). The AF performance seemed to improve after the firmware update that was installed via the desktop app before testing fully commenced.

This functionality isn’t, of course, relevant to astrophotography, but it’s still a useful point to mention in case you intend to use the lens with autofocus in the day. Focusing is also internal, so the front element doesn’t rotate during focusing like cheap and cheerful kit lenses.

The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) was tested with the Sony A7R V, which offers an unforgivingly high resolution. The lens was tested at night with a focus on astrophotography, and in daylight to assess sharpness, distortion and general functionality for an all-round approach to testing.

Online reviews echo one another, praising the AF 35mm f/1.8 for its sharpness and cost. Users appreciate that while it’s certainly not in the league of Sony’s premium G Master lenses, it represents great value for money. Some reviewers mention great build quality and looking good when paired with their Sony camera.

✅ You’re on a tight budget: The price of this lens is extremely attractive given the specs and performance.

✅ You want portability: This is a compact and lightweight lens that's much less bulky than faster primes.

❌ You want the best: This is a great little lens in many ways, but its image quality isn't the best that money can buy.

❌ You shoot APS-C: Unless this is what you want, the equivalent focal length on a crop sensor is 52.5mm

Prime lenses can be expensive, especially if you’re looking at those with an f/1.4 or f/1.2 maximum aperture. The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) is a budget option in the Viltrox line-up, but with decent overall performance alongside impressive image quality for the price, this is a great 35mm lens for those on a budget. It’s also compact and lightweight, which could be useful if you often head out shooting with several lenses in your kit bag.

Just going back to image quality, images are sharp, but when shooting astrophotography at f/1.8, there was some astigmatism at the left edges of the frame. This is where stars appear as crosses. You can only really see this when you zoom in to 100%, but it’s worth bearing in mind if you’re looking for the closest to optical perfection you can find.

When a weather-sealed prime lens with a manual aperture ring costs just $399 / £385, you can’t help but take notice. Build quality is excellent and the lens undoubtedly looks and feels like it would be more expensive than it is.

Considering all of this and the image quality, the lens is fairly priced and is still at the release price, so it could become more affordable in the future. Just like other Viltrox lenses, in the box you get the lens, a lens hood, front and rear lens caps and a soft lens case.

The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.2 LAB FE is part of Viltrox’s flagship lens series and offers a much faster maximum aperture, as the name suggests. It’s also more expensive, larger and heavier.

If you’d like a wider lens, the Sony FE 20mm f/1.8 G is a fantastic option offering exceptional image quality alongside a compact build and light weight. A potential must-have for Sony users.

If you’d like to go wider still, the Sigma 14mm f/1.4 DG DN Art is an absolute beast of a lens, offering an ultra-wide light-gathering field of view alongside a fast f/1.4 maximum aperture.

James is an award-winning freelance landscape and portrait photographer, as well as a highly experienced photography journalist working with some of the best photography magazines and websites with a worldwide audience. He’s also the author of The Digital Darkroom: The Definitive Guide to Photo Editing. www.jamesaphoto.co.uk

#586. Evacuation from Oleshky: How are preparations going?

A lawyer with the Save Ukraine Foundation, Myroslava Kharchenko, told DW about what has been happening in Russian-occupied Oleshky since a temporary ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump took effect.

Since a ceasefire took effect in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region on October 27, preparations have been underway to evacuate residents trapped there.

Following Russia's occupation of the town in 2022 and the flooding caused by the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka dam in 2023, residents were cut off from the outside world. All access routes to Oleshky, which lies on the Dnipro River, had been mined. Former Oleshky residents who managed to escape and talked to DW described hunger, no access to medicine, and no electricity or water. About 2,000 people are still living in the town.

According to the Save Ukraine Foundation, it has rescued at least 300 civilians from Oleshky over the past six months. DW spoke with lawyer Myroslava Kharchenko, who works for the organization, about preparations for the upcoming evacuation.

DW: A ceasefire is already in effect in Oleshky. Do you know whether any evacuation efforts have begun?

Myroslava Kharchenko: No, we do not have that information yet. What we do know is that the ceasefire came into effect on October 27 at 3 a.m. Kyiv time, which is 4 a.m. in Russia. Mine-clearing operations on the road began at around 8 a.m. What is happening inside Oleshky itself, however, is entirely within the military's remit. Everyone involved in this operation has been asked to maintain strict confidentiality. Any careless remark or action could jeopardize the entire evacuation effort.

What I can see is that information is being actively collected through closed internal local chat groups. Registration lists and application forms are being shared, and people are filling them out themselves. Organizers are contacting those who previously requested evacuation to verify details such as their date of birth and current place of residence. They are also asking people to provide contact information for neighbors or relatives who may be nearby or in the same building, because communications are extremely unreliable.

The organizers are also collecting information about the health conditions of those planning to leave. Among them are people who are ill, have limited mobility, or are recovering from recent injuries, including blast and mine-related wounds. We therefore expect those organizing the evacuation to ensure that medical assistance is available for those who need it.

How exactly is the evacuation expected to take place? Will people be evacuated through Russian-controlled territory or via the Dnipro River? Have any routes already been agreed upon?

As far as we know, a river route would be extremely dangerous. We have not heard any confirmation that such an option has been approved. It therefore appears likely that the evacuation route will pass through the temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory and possibly through Russia before people are able to reach Ukraine. For security reasons, however, none of these details are being made public.

What do you know about the number of people expected to be evacuated?

We are actually very pleased that the evacuation is not expected to take place in a single day. That is important because we hope that those who manage to leave safely during the first stage will serve as an example for others.

People still trapped in Oleshky are extremely afraid. There have already been numerous provocations, and this is not the first attempt to establish such a route or humanitarian corridor.

As a result, there is a great deal of suspicion. Those concerns are based largely on uncertainty, and some people may choose not to leave during the initial phase of the evacuation. Overall, however, we estimate that around 500 people may eventually be evacuated.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How would you assess the role of Melania Trump in making this evacuation possible?

We are immensely grateful to Melania Trump for drawing attention to the humanitarian catastrophe currently unfolding in Oleshky. What is taking place there is in fact genocide committed by the Russian Federation.

We are thankful for her efforts and hope they will help make this evacuation possible. We will be even more grateful once most people are safely removed from the combat zone and arrive in Ukrainian government-controlled territory.

When could the physical evacuation of civilians begin?

I can't say how long it will take. What seems clear, however, is that time will be needed to clear mines from the roads leading into the city. We also understand that many streets inside Oleshky are mined, so additional work will be required to make routes within the city safe.

There is a hospital from which people need to be evacuated. Nearby is a morgue where bodies also need to be recovered.

I do not know whether that will be included as part of this humanitarian corridor, but it is undoubtedly important. The bodies need to be identified and the causes of death established. That process will also take time, regardless of how quickly the military is able to work.

It is difficult to make any predictions because, as you can see, everything is being conducted under strict secrecy. Statements from both the Russian and Ukrainian sides have been extremely cautious, and that is clearly justified under the circumstances.

#585. Large Hadron Collider reveals evidence of Big Bang matter in surprisingly small collisions

The findings come one year after the first-ever oxygen collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). All four of the collider's major research collaborations, ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and LHCb, have now reported signs that this primordial form of matter can emerge when oxygen and neon nuclei collide.

The findings come one year after the first-ever oxygen collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). All four of the collider's major research collaborations, ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and LHCb, have now reported signs that this primordial form of matter can emerge when oxygen and neon nuclei collide.

The results challenge a long-standing assumption about the enormous forces needed to create such an extreme substance. They also offer scientists a new way to investigate the conditions that prevailed during the universe's earliest moments.

Quark–gluon plasma (QGP) is an unusual state of matter that appears under tremendous pressure and heat. At temperatures exceeding 100,000 times those at the Sun's center, particles such as protons and neutrons can no longer maintain their normal structure. Instead, they break apart into quarks and the gluons that ordinarily bind them together.

Physicists believe that this was the state of matter throughout the universe during the first millionths of a second after the Big Bang. Nearly 14 billion years later, researchers can briefly recreate these extraordinary conditions by smashing atomic nuclei together at extremely high energies inside the LHC.

For decades, scientists believed that generating this plasma required collisions involving very heavy atomic nuclei, particularly lead. Lead nuclei are more than 200 times heavier than the protons typically used in LHC experiments, making them capable of producing the intense conditions thought necessary for QGP to form.

However, recent discoveries have increasingly called that assumption into question.

Earlier this year, the ALICE collaboration, which specializes in studying quark–gluon plasma, identified another indication of QGP formation in proton–proton and proton–lead collisions. The previous year, LHC researchers had also reported the first hints of this plasma emerging from oxygen–oxygen collisions.

Now, more detailed investigations have revealed multiple signs that QGP can form in collisions involving both oxygen and neon nuclei, providing stronger evidence that the conditions required to create this primordial matter are not limited to heavy atomic collisions.

One of the clearest ways to identify quark–gluon plasma is to examine what happens when energetic quarks and gluons travel through it.

As these particles move through the extremely hot and dense material, they lose some of their energy. Scientists call this process parton energy loss, and it provides an important clue that QGP has formed.

The ATLAS collaboration clearly detected this effect by studying pairs of particle jets generated during oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions. These jets are concentrated streams of particles produced when energetic quarks and gluons emerge from a collision.

Researchers observed differences in energy between the paired jets, indicating that some of the particles had lost energy while traveling through the surrounding material.

The effect was especially pronounced during more direct, head-on (central) collisions. Such impacts are expected to create a larger volume of plasma, giving particles more material to travel through and causing greater energy loss.

Preliminary ATLAS results provide additional support for this interpretation. By examining charged particles that recoil in the opposite direction from photons, researchers found a similar relationship between energy loss and how centrally the nuclei collided.

The ALICE, CMS, and LHCb collaborations searched for the same underlying process using a different approach. Rather than focusing primarily on the energy of particle jets, they examined how the plasma appears to reduce the production of certain energetic particles.

CMS found that charged-particle production was suppressed in both oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions compared with proton–proton collisions. This reduction is consistent with particles losing energy inside quark–gluon plasma and provides further evidence that the exotic material can form in collisions involving lighter nuclei.

LHCb reported another important clue in a separate study. The collaboration investigated particles containing a charm quark and a lighter quark, comparing how strongly their production was suppressed in oxygen and neon collisions.

The suppression was more pronounced in the heavier neon collisions. That is precisely the kind of behavior scientists would expect if larger collisions produce greater volumes of plasma, causing particles to lose more energy as they pass through it.

However, reduced particle production does not necessarily prove that energy loss is responsible. Other physical processes could potentially produce similar effects.

To investigate this possibility, ALICE compared the production of neutral pions, another type of subatomic particle, in oxygen–oxygen and proton–oxygen collisions.

The comparison provided unambiguous evidence of parton energy loss in oxygen–oxygen collisions, strengthening the case that even relatively small nuclear collisions can generate conditions associated with quark–gluon plasma.

Researchers also looked for another distinctive signature of QGP involving particles made from a heavy quark and its corresponding antiquark.

These pairs can briefly bind together following high-energy collisions. Some are more tightly bound than others, making them differently susceptible to disruption by the surrounding plasma.

By examining which bound states are suppressed and by how much, physicists can gather additional evidence about whether QGP is present.

The CMS collaboration found evidence of this varying suppression in particles called upsilon mesons, which consist of a bottom quark paired with its antiquark. The researchers identified the effect by comparing oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions.

LHCb also reported preliminary evidence of similar behavior, this time using data from proton–oxygen and oxygen–oxygen collisions.

Together, these observations add another piece to the growing body of evidence that primordial plasma can emerge in nuclear collisions much smaller than those traditionally used to study it.

The ALICE collaboration has identified yet another possible signature of quark–gluon plasma, this time involving the directions in which particles travel after a collision.

In preliminary findings, researchers observed that particles containing three quarks (baryons) showed a stronger preference for certain directions than particles composed of two quarks (mesons) during oxygen–oxygen collisions.

This behavior is known as anisotropic flow. Rather than spreading evenly in every direction, particles emerge in patterns influenced by the conditions inside the material created during the collision.

The leading explanation involves the formation of QGP. When particles with intermediate momenta emerge from this plasma, they can inherit collective motion from the quarks that make them up.

Because baryons contain three quarks while mesons contain only two, baryons can inherit more of this flow, producing the difference observed in the experiment.

This distinctive pattern provides another potential indication that the extreme matter of the early universe is being recreated in oxygen collisions.

Scientists are continuing to analyze data from collisions involving lighter atomic nuclei, searching for additional evidence of how quark–gluon plasma forms and behaves.

The findings are reshaping the understanding of the conditions needed to produce one of the most extreme states of matter known to physics. What once appeared to require collisions between massive nuclei can now be investigated through much smaller systems, giving researchers new opportunities to explore the behavior of matter under extraordinary conditions.

Meanwhile, CERN is upgrading the Large Hadron Collider into the more powerful High-Luminosity LHC. The enhanced accelerator will allow scientists to collect substantially more collision data and investigate the properties of quark–gluon plasma in greater detail.

With each new discovery, researchers are gaining a clearer picture of the remarkable state of matter that dominated the universe during its first fleeting moments after the Big Bang.
